p.seg: Xiāoyáoyóu Dì Yī
In the Northern Ocean, there is a fish,
its name is Kūn.
The Kūn's size,
no one knows how many thousands of miles it is.
It transforms into a bird,
its name is Péng.
The Péng's back,
no one knows how many thousands of miles it is;
when it rages and flies,
its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky.
This bird,
By sea, it will then migrate to Nán Míng.
Nán Míng is the celestial pond.
Qí Xié was,
a recorder of marvels.
He said:
"When the Péng migrates to Nán Míng,
it strikes the water for three thousand *lǐ*,
whirling upwards ninety thousand *lǐ* on a cyclone,
departing with the June winds."
The roaming dust-like mist,
the floating dust,
are blown about by the breath of living creatures.
The blueness of the sky,
is that its true color?
Or is it so far that there is no end to its extent?
When it looks down below,
it probably sees things in the same way.
Furthermore, if the accumulation of water is not deep,
then it will not have the strength to bear a large boat.
Pour a cup of water in a depression in the hall floor,
and a mustard seed will be a boat for it;
put a cup in it, and it will stick,
because the water is shallow and the boat is large.
If the accumulation of wind is not deep,
then it will not have the strength to bear a large wing.
Therefore, to rise ninety thousand *lǐ*,
Then the wind is pressing below,
and only then does it gather strength;
carrying the blue sky on its back, // with nothing to cut it short,
and only then does it plan to fly south.
The cicada and the dove laugh at it, saying:
"I leap up and fly,
bumping into elms and rafters,
sometimes not even reaching them, // but simply landing on the ground;
why go ninety thousand *lǐ* to the south?"
He who goes to the nearby wilds
returns with three meals,
his stomach still full;
he who goes a hundred *lǐ*
pounds grain overnight;
he who goes a thousand *lǐ*
gathers provisions for three months.
What do these two insects know!
Small knowledge does not reach great knowledge,
a short lifespan does not reach a long lifespan.
How do we know that this is so?
The morning mushroom does not know morning and dusk,
the cicada does not know spring and autumn;
these are short lifespans.
South of Chǔ is Mínglíng,
who takes five hundred years for a spring,
and five hundred years for an autumn;
in ancient times there was Dàchūn,
who takes eight thousand years for a spring,
and eight thousand years for an autumn.
Yet Péngzǔ is now uniquely known for his longevity;
the multitude try to match him,
is it not sad!
Enjoying carefree slumber beneath it.
It is not cut down by axes,
no creature harms it,
it is of no use,
how could it be troubled by hardship!"
*Qíwù Lùn* (Discourse on Seeing Things as Equal) - Second
Nánguō Zǐqí leaned on his armrest and sat,
looking up at the sky and sighing.
He seemed utterly lost, as though he had lost his companion.
Yánchéng Zǐyóu stood in attendance before him,
and said:
"What is this?
Can the body truly be made like withered wood,
and can the heart truly be made like dead ashes?
He who leans on his armrest now
is not the same as he who leaned on his armrest in the past."
Zǐqí said:
"Yǎn, is it not good that you ask about this!
Just now, I lost myself.
Do you understand this?
You have heard the music of man
but have not yet heard the music of earth.
You have heard the music of earth
but have not yet heard the music of heaven!"
Zǐyóu said:
"May I venture to ask about its meaning?"
Zǐqí said:
"The Great Clod breathes out breath,
its name is wind.
When it does not act, that is all;
but when it acts, myriad apertures roar in anger.
Have you not heard it whistling loudly?
In the mountain forests,
it is fate!"
Chapter Seven: Ruling Emperors and Kings
Niè Quē asked Wáng Nì,
four questions, and four times he did not know.
Niè Quē then jumped for joy
and went to tell Púyī Zǐ.
Púyī Zǐ said,
"Do you now understand it?
The Yǒu Yú clan (Shùn) is inferior to the Tàishì clan.
The Yǒu Yú clan,
they are like hoarding benevolence to coerce people;
they also obtained people,
but never emerged from the inhuman.
The Tàishì clan, when they slept, they were leisurely;
when they woke, they were carefree;
sometimes they regarded themselves as horses,
sometimes they regarded themselves as cows;
their knowledge and emotions were genuine,
their virtue was exceedingly true,
and they never entered into the inhuman."
Jiān Wú met Kuáng Jiēyú.
Kuáng Jiēyú said,
"What did Rì Zhōng tell you?"
Jiān Wú said,
"He told me
that the ruler should set forth
constant models, righteous standards, and measurements,
so who would dare not listen and be transformed!"
Jiē Yú said:
"This is deceiving virtue.
As for governing the world,
it's like dredging a river in the sea
or having mosquitoes carry a mountain.
The sage's governance,
is it governing externally?
Correcting oneself and then acting,
only those who are certain they can do the job should do it.
Furthermore, birds fly high
to avoid the harm of arrows and tethered arrows,
and voles burrow deep under the sacred mounds
to avoid the calamity of smoke and digging.
And yet you surpass these two ignorant insects!"
Tiān Gēn wandered in Yīn Yáng,
arriving at the banks of the Liǎo River.
He happened to meet a nameless person and asked him,
saying,
"May I ask about governing the world?"
The nameless person said,
"Go away!
You are a vulgar person,
why do you ask such unpleasant questions!
I am about to become a companion to the Creator,
when I am sated,
I will then ride the Mǎngmiǎo bird,
to go beyond the six limits,
and wander in the land of "nothing whatsoever,"
to dwell in the vast wilderness.
How could you have the leisure
to govern the world and move my heart?"
He asked again.
Wú Míng Rén said:
"If you roam your mind in tranquility,
harmonize your Qi in stillness,
follow the natural course of things
and have no selfish desires,
then the world will be governed."
Yáng Zǐ Jū met Lǎo Dān,
and said:
"There is a man here,
who is quick and strong,
discerning and intelligent,
and tirelessly learns the Dao.
Can such a person
be compared to an enlightened ruler?"
Lǎo Dān said:
"In relation to a sage,
he is merely
a skilled craftsman,
someone who labors his body and alarms his heart.
Furthermore, the patterns of tigers and leopards attract hunters,
and the agility of monkeys
brings dogs with leashes.
Is one who does this
comparable to a wise ruler?"
Yáng Zǐjū started in surprise and said,
"May I venture to ask about the government of a wise ruler?"
Lǎo Dān said,
"The government of a wise ruler is such that,
his achievements cover the world
yet appear not to be his own,
Many females without a male,
how can they produce eggs?
If you use the Dao to contend with the world,
insisting on being believed,
it is precisely this that allows people to assess you.
Try to bring him again,
and show him to me."
The next day, Lièzǐ brought him to see Húzǐ.
After coming out, he said to Lièzǐ:
"Alas!
Your teacher is as good as dead!
He won't live!
It won't be more than ten days!
I saw strangeness in him, I saw damp ashes."
Lièzǐ went in,
with tears wetting his lapels, and told Húzǐ.
Húzǐ said:
"Just now, I showed him the pattern of the earth,
budding forth, neither shaking nor stopping.
He probably saw my
mechanism of stifled virtue.
Try to bring him again."
The next day,
he brought him again to see Húzǐ.
After coming out, he said to Lièzǐ:
"Lucky for your teacher that he met me!
He has a chance of recovery,
he has the semblance of life!
"I saw his Dù Quán."
Lièzǐ entered,
and told Húzǐ.
Húzǐ said:
"Just now, I showed him Tiānrǎng,
where names and realities do not enter,
and the mechanism was triggered at the heel.
He probably saw in me the mechanism of goodness.
Try bringing him again."
The next day,
he again brought him to see Húzǐ.
Coming out, he said to Lièzǐ:
"Your master is not aligned;
I have no way to observe him.
Try to align him,
and then I will observe him again."
Lièzǐ entered,
and told Húzǐ.
Húzǐ said:
"Just now, I showed him Tài Chōng, which nothing can overcome.
He probably saw in me the mechanism of balanced qi.
The careful consideration of the salamander creates a deep pool,
the careful consideration of still water creates a deep pool,
the careful consideration of flowing water creates a deep pool.
The deep pool has nine names;
this place contains three of them.
Try bringing him again."
The next day,
Then he (Lièzǐ) again went with him to see Húzi.
Before he (Lièzǐ) had even stood firmly,
he (Jiǎodǐ) lost himself and ran away.
Húzi said, "Chase after him!"
Lièzǐ chased after him but could not catch up.
Returning, he reported to Húzi, saying,
"He has vanished,
he is lost,
I could not reach him."
Húzi said,
"Just now, I showed him that I had not yet begun to reveal my true nature.
I dealt with him vacantly and compliantly,
not knowing who he was,
and consequently treating him as declining,
and consequently as a flowing wave,
therefore he fled."
After this, Lièzǐ considered himself to have never begun learning
and returned home,
not going out for three years.
He cooked for his wife,
and fed pigs as if he were feeding people.
He was intimate with no affairs,
and his carved ornaments returned to plainness.
He stood alone, solid as a clod of earth, simply existing in his form.
Amidst the confusion, he remained complete,
and he ended things consistently.
He did not act as a master of reputation,
nor a planner of schemes;
To act without being involved in affairs,
to know without being a master.
To embody the inexhaustible,
and to wander without trace;
to exhaust what is received from Heaven,
and to have no perception of attainment,
is merely emptiness.
The mind of the ultimate person is like a mirror,
neither escorting nor welcoming,
responding but not storing,
therefore able to overcome things without being harmed.
The emperor of the South Sea was Shū,
the emperor of the North Sea was Hū,
and the emperor of the Center was Hùndùn.
Shū and Hū often met in the land of Hùndùn,
and Hùndùn treated them very well.
Shū and Hū plotted to repay Hùndùn's kindness,
saying, "Everyone has seven orifices
for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing,
but this one alone has none;
let's try to bore them."
They bored one orifice each day,
and in seven days Hùndùn died.
"Webbed Toes" - Eighth
Webbed toes and extra fingers
are they from nature?
And extravagance in virtue.
Superfluous growths and hanging tumors,
do they come from the (external) form?
And extravagance in nature.
The abundance of benevolence and righteousness and those who employ them,
are they arrayed in the five viscera?
And they are not the correctness of morality.
Therefore, those with webbed feet
have connected, useless flesh;
those with extra fingers on their hands
grow useless digits;
to have various kinds of excrescences connected to the emotions of the five viscera
is to be excessive and perverse in the practice of benevolence and righteousness,
and to be excessive in the use of intelligence.
Therefore, those with excess of sight
confound the five colors,
and are excessive in ornamentation.
Is it not the dazzling brilliance of blue, yellow, and embroidered silks?
And Lí Zhū is an example of this.
Those with an excess of hearing
confound the five tones,
and are excessive in the six musical pitches, the sounds of metal, stone, strings, bamboo, the yellow bell and the great Lü?
And Shī Kuàng is an example of this.
Those who grow excessive in benevolence
diminish virtue and block up nature
in order to gather fame and reputation,
causing the world to beat drums
Is it wrong to employ methods that are beyond one's reach?
Zēng Shēn 曾參 and Shǐ Yú 石魚 are examples of this.
Those who are fixated on argument,
piling up tiles, knotting ropes to create sentences,
letting their minds wander amongst the distinctions of "hard and white" and "sameness and difference,"
is it wrong to exhaust their steps in pursuit of useless words?
Yáng Zhū 楊朱 and Mò Dí 墨翟 are examples of this.
Therefore, all these are branching, side-paths,
and not the utmost correctness of the world.
That which is utmost correctness
does not lose the essence of its inherent nature.
Therefore, what is complete does not need to be pieced together,
and what is branched does not need to be divided;
what is long is not considered excessive,
and what is short is not considered insufficient.
Therefore, though a duck's leg is short,
extending it would cause distress;
though a crane's leg is long,
cutting it would cause sorrow.
Thus, what is inherently long should not be cut,
and what is inherently short should not be extended,
so that there is no cause for worry.
Do you mean to say that benevolence and righteousness are not human emotions?
Why are those benevolent people so full of worries?
Furthermore, a sixth toe that is joined to the thumb,
cutting it off will cause weeping;
an extra finger growing from the hand,
If one bites them, they will cry.
These two [situations],
sometimes have an excess in number,
sometimes have a deficiency in number,
their concern is the same.
The benevolent people of today,
with strained eyes, worry about the troubles of the world;
the unbenevolent people,
sever the emotions of life and greedily pursue nobility and wealth.
Intentionally making benevolence and righteousness something that is not human nature!
Since the Three Dynasties and later,
how clamorous the world is!
Moreover, to wait for hooks, lines, compasses, and squares to correct things,
is to pare away at their nature;
to wait for ropes and glue to make things firm,
is to encroach upon their virtue;
bending and twisting rites and music,
loudly advocating benevolence and righteousness,
in order to comfort the hearts of the world,
this is to lose their natural state.
The world has a natural state.
The natural state is that
crooked things are not straightened with hooks,
straight things are not straightened with lines,
A circle is not (made) with a compass;
a square is not (made) with a T-square;
adhesion does not rely on glue and lacquer;
constraint does not rely on ropes.
Therefore, all under Heaven are induced to be born
without knowing why they are born;
they all obtain equally
without knowing how they obtain.
Thus, ancient and modern are not different;
it cannot be diminished.
This is what is called the transformation of things.
Yǎngshēng Zhǔ (Nourishing Life) Third
My life has a limit,
but knowledge has no limit.
To use the limited to pursue the unlimited is dangerous;
if, knowing this is dangerous, one still pursues knowledge, then one is truly in danger.
In doing good, do not seek fame;
in doing evil, do not approach punishment.
Follow the central vein as the constant path,
and you can protect your body,
you can keep your life whole,
you can nourish your parents,
you can live out your years.
Cook Dīng (Páo Dīng) was butchering an ox for Lord Wénhuì (Wénhuì Jūn).
Wherever his hand touched,
wherever his shoulder leaned,
wherever his foot stepped,
wherever his knee pressed,
with a ripping sound and a whooshing sound,
the blade made a slicing sound,
everything was in perfect harmony.
It matched the dance of the "Sāng Lín,"
and was in accord with the music of the "Jīng Shǒu."
Lord Wénhuì (Wénhuì Jūn) said, "Ah, excellent!
Has your skill reached such a point?"
Cook Dīng (Páo Dīng) laid down his knife and replied,
"What your servant loves is the Dao,
It has advanced to skill.
At the beginning, when I, your servant, was butchering oxen,
what I saw was nothing but the ox.
After three years, I never saw the whole ox anymore.
Now, at this time,
I meet [the ox] with my spirit
and do not look at it with my eyes.
The senses stop working
but the spirit wants to move.
I rely on the natural principles,
strike into the large crevices,
guide [the knife] through the large cavities,
and follow its inherent structure.
I never touch the tendons or bones, let alone the large bones!
A good cook changes his knife every year because he cuts [meat];
a common cook changes his knife every month because he hacks [meat].
Now, my knife has been used for nineteen years;
I have butchered thousands of oxen with it;
yet the blade is as sharp as if it had just been sharpened on a whetstone.
Because the joints have spaces between them,
and the blade has no thickness;
with what has no thickness, I enter into the spaces;
how freely
there is surely room for the blade to move about!
Therefore, after nineteen years, the blade is as if newly sharpened on a whetstone.
Although this is so, whenever I come to a complicated joint,
I see the difficulty in it,
and I am filled with caution and take warning.
My gaze is fixed,
and my movements are slow.
The movement of the knife is extremely subtle,
yet with a "huò" sound, it is already separated,
like earth falling to the ground.
I stand holding the knife,
and for this, I look around in all directions,
and for this, I linger, filled with self-satisfaction,
and carefully clean the knife and put it away."
Wén Huì Jūn said, "Excellent!
Having heard the words of the cook Ding,
I have learned how to nourish life."
Gōng Wénxuān saw the Right Master
and exclaimed in astonishment,
"Who is this person?
Why is he missing a foot?
Is it the work of Heaven, or of man?"
The reply was: "It is Heaven, not man.
Heaven creates him to be unique,
while human appearance involves having companions.
From this, we know that it is Heaven,
not man.
A swamp pheasant pecks once every ten steps,
and drinks once every hundred steps,
不 qī chù hū fán zhōng. "Not hoping to be kept like an animal in a pen."
Shén suī wáng, bù shàn yě." "Though a spirit is king, it is not good."
When Lǎo Dān died, Qín Shī went to offer condolences,
cried out three times, and left.
A disciple said, "Was he not a friend of our master?"
He said:
"He was."
"Then is it proper to offer condolences in this way?"
He said, "It is.
At first, I thought he was the right kind of person,
but now he is not.
Just now I went in to offer condolences,
and there was an old man weeping for him as if he were his son;
a young man weeping for him as if he were his mother.
The way they were gathered there for him
must have involved those who spoke without meaning to speak,
and wept without meaning to weep.
This is escaping from Heaven and turning one's back on true feelings,
forgetting what one has received.
The ancients called this the punishment of escaping from Heaven.
When he came, it was the master's time;
when he left, it was the master's compliance.
Being content with time and dwelling in compliance,
sorrow and joy cannot enter.
The ancients called this being released by God."
The kindling may be exhausted,
but the fire is passed on, and its end is unknown.
Chapter 4: Réngān Shì (In the World of Men)
Yán Huí saw Zhòng Ní and
requested to leave.
Zhòng Ní asked,
"Where are you going?"
Yán Huí replied,
"I am going to Wèi."
Zhòng Ní asked,
"What for?"
Yán Huí replied,
"I have heard that the ruler of Wèi
is young,
and his actions are reckless.
He uses his country lightly
and does not see his own faults.
He treats the death of the people lightly;
the dead in the country lie heaped in the marshes like rushes.
The people probably have no recourse.
I once heard you say, Master,
'Leave a well-governed country,
go to a disordered country;
the doctor's door has many illnesses.'
I wish to use what I have learned to consider their principles,
hoping that their country may be healed!"
Zhòng Ní said,
"Alas!
You will probably go and be punished!
For the Dao does not like to be mixed;
Mixed (things) are many;
when there are many, there is disturbance;
when there is disturbance, there is worry;
if one worries and does not remedy (the situation).
The ultimate person of ancient times
first cultivated (virtue) within themselves
and only then cultivated it in others.
If what is cultivated within oneself is not yet established,
how can one have the leisure to address the actions of violent people!
Furthermore, do you also know where virtue is undermined
and where knowledge comes from?
Virtue is undermined by reputation;
knowledge comes from contention.
Reputation is that by which people attack each other;
knowledge is the tool of contention.
These two are dangerous tools,
not those by which (one should) fully conduct oneself.
Furthermore, if one's virtue is substantial and one's trust is firm,
but one has not grasped human nature,
and one's reputation is heard without contention,
but one has not grasped the human heart;
and if one forcibly uses the language of benevolence, righteousness, rules, and laws to instruct violent people,
this is (because) people resent having their good qualities mentioned;
this is called harming people.
One who harms people
will inevitably be harmed in return;
you will likely be harmed by others!
Furthermore, if one merely likes the virtuous and dislikes the unworthy,
Why strive to be different through the misuse of power?
If you simply issue no commands,
the kings and dukes will surely take advantage of others
and compete in their quickness.
Your eyes will be dazzled by it,
your countenance will be placated by it,
your mouth will be managed by it,
your demeanor will be shaped by it,
and your mind will be consumed by it.
This is like using fire to put out fire,
using water to put out water,
which is called making it even more.
Following this path will lead to endless troubles.
If you are likely to rely on insincere and verbose words,
you will surely die before violent men!
Moreover, in the past, Jié 桀 killed Guān Lóngféng 關龍逢,
Zhòu 紂 killed Prince Bǐgān 比干.
These were all men who cultivated themselves
to care for the people,
and used their inferior status to oppose their superiors.
Therefore, their rulers used their virtue to eliminate them.
These were those who loved fame.
In the past, Yáo 堯 attacked Cóngzhī 叢枝 and Xū'áo 胥敖,
Yǔ 禹 attacked Yǒuhù 有扈.
The states became empty and desolate,
and they themselves faced punishment and execution.
Their use of military force did not stop,
their pursuit of practical results was endless.
These are all people who seek fame and reality.
But have you alone not heard of it?
Fame and reality are things that even the sages cannot overcome.
How much less can you!
However,
if you must have a way,
try telling me about it!"
Yán Huí said:
"Be upright and humble,
diligent and focused.
Would that be acceptable?"
The other said:
"Oh! How could that be acceptable!
To fill oneself with a proud and boastful manner,
with fluctuating expressions and emotions,
never disagreeing with ordinary people,
and catering to people's feelings,
seeking to accommodate their hearts,
calling it
'gradual virtue',
this will not lead to success,
much less to great virtue!
You will be stubborn and unyielding,
outwardly conforming
but inwardly not criticizing.
How could that possibly work!"
"Then, how about I am inwardly upright but outwardly yielding,
achieving success and emulating those above?
One who is inwardly upright
takes Heaven as their companion.
One who takes Heaven as their companion
knows that both the Son of Heaven and oneself are children of Heaven.
Why should one seek to have others approve of one's words,
or seek to have others disapprove of them?
If so,
people will call such a person a child.
This is what it means to take Heaven as one's companion.
One who is outwardly compliant
takes people as their companion.
Holding things high, kneeling, bowing low—
these are the rituals of a minister.
Everyone does them,
how dare I not do them?
Doing what others do
leaves one without fault.
This is what it means to take people as one's companion.
One who completes their work and then makes comparisons to superiors
takes the ancients as their companion.
Even if their words instruct, they are in reality censuring.
What the ancients possessed
is not what I possess.
If so,
even if one is straightforward, there is no harm.
This is what it means to take the ancients as one's companion.
Would this be acceptable?"
Zhòng Ní said:
"Alas! Alas!"
"Most great administrations and laws
do not use spies.
Though they are firm, there is also no fault.
Even so, they only stop there.
How can this reach transformation!
It is like those who take themselves as their teacher."
Yán Huí 顏回 said:
"I have no way to progress;
may I venture to ask the method?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"Fast, and I will tell you!
To have something and act on it, is it easy?
For those who deem it easy,
brilliant Heaven will not approve."
Yán Huí 顏回 said:
"My family is poor;
I only refrain from drinking wine and eating meat
for several months.
Like this, can I consider it fasting?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"That is the fast for sacrifices; it is not the fasting of the mind."
Yán Huí 顏回 said:
"May I venture to ask about the fasting of the mind?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"If you unify your will,
do not listen with your ears,
but listen with your mind;
Do not listen with your mind,
but listen with your *qi*!
Listening stops at the ear,
the mind stops at symbols.
*Qi* is
that which is empty and waits for things.
Only the Dao gathers in emptiness.
Emptiness is the fasting of the mind."
Yán Huí said:
"When I had not yet begun to receive the instruction,
it was indeed myself [that was present];
having received the instruction,
there was no longer any myself [present];
can this be called emptiness?"
The Master said:
"You have exhausted it.
I will tell you!
If you can enter and roam within its enclosure
and not be affected by its fame,
when you enter, you will resonate;
when you do not enter, you will stop.
With no gate and no obstruction,
dwelling in a single abode of necessity,
then you are close [to the Dao].
Cutting off footprints is easy,
but walking without touching the ground is difficult.
Being employed by men is easy with pretense,
but being employed by Heaven is difficult with pretense.
I have heard of flying with wings,
but I have never heard of flying without wings.
I have heard of knowing with knowledge,
but I have never heard of knowing without knowledge.
Look at that empty chamber:
in an empty room, whiteness is born,
and good fortune abides.
If it does not abide,
this is called "sitting and galloping."
When one follows what the ears and eyes perceive internally,
while remaining externally aloof from the mind's knowledge,
spirits and gods will come to dwell,
how much more so people!
This is what transforms all things,
what Yǔ and Shùn grasped,
and what Fúxī and Jīqú ultimately practiced.
How much more so those who are scattered!"
Yè Gōngzǐ Gāo was about to be sent as an envoy to Qí,
and asked Zhòngní, saying:
"The king's mission to me regarding Liáng is very important.
Qí's treatment of envoys
will probably be very respectful but not urgent.
Even a commoner cannot be easily moved,
how much more so a feudal lord!
I am very afraid of this.
You once said to me regarding Liáng:
'In all matters, whether small or large,
there are few that do not achieve harmony through improper means.
Few can achieve joy through unprincipled behavior.
If a matter is not accomplished,
then there will surely be the trouble of human affairs;
if a matter is accomplished,
then there will surely be the trouble of *yīn* and *yáng*.
Only one with virtue can accomplish (a thing) or not accomplish it and thereafter have no troubles.'"
Only the virtuous can do this.
I eat, holding to coarse food and not finding it good,
(my) cooking has no one who desires purity.
Now I receive my orders in the morning
and drink ice in the evening;
I must be internally feverish!
I have not yet reached the true state of affairs,
and already there is the trouble of *yīn* and *yáng*;
if the matter is not accomplished,
there will surely be the trouble of human affairs.
These are two (difficulties),
a minister is not adequate to bear them;
may you have something to tell me about them!"
Zhòng Ní said:
"In the world there are two great prohibitions:
the first is fate;
the second is righteousness.
Your love for your parents
is fate;
it cannot be loosened from your heart.
A minister's service to his ruler
is righteousness;
There is no place where you are not in the presence of the ruler,
and there is nowhere to escape within the confines of heaven and earth.
This is called a great precept.
Therefore, those who serve their parents,
do not choose a place to find peace there;
this is the ultimate filial piety.
Those who serve their ruler,
do not choose the task to find peace in it;
this is the perfection of loyalty.
Those who govern their own hearts,
do not allow grief or joy to easily influence them;
knowing that there is nothing one can do
they accept it as fate,
this is the ultimate virtue.
Those who are ministers and sons,
invariably have circumstances beyond their control.
If one focuses on the reality of the action
and forgets oneself,
how can they have time to delight in life and abhor death!
Master, your conduct is acceptable!
Qiū (丘) will repeat what I have heard:
In all interactions,
those who are near must use sincerity to establish trust,
those who are far must use loyalty in their words,
and words must be passed on by someone.
To pass on words of both joy and anger,
is the most difficult thing in the world.
When there is shared joy,
Surely there will be many words of excessive praise;
when two are angry
surely there will be many words of excessive condemnation.
All kinds of excess are falsehoods;
if they are false, then they are scarcely believed;
if they are scarcely believed, then those who spread such words invite disaster.
Therefore, the *Fǎ Yán* says:
"Transmit the usual circumstances,
do not transmit the excessive words,
then you are almost whole."
Furthermore, those who fight with skill against strength
begin with the *yáng*,
and usually end with the *yīn*;
when flourishing reaches its peak, there will be many strange and clever techniques.
Those who drink wine with propriety
begin with order,
and usually end with chaos;
when flourishing reaches its peak, there will be much strange merriment.
All things are also like this.
They begin with trust,
and usually end with meanness;
their beginnings are simple,
but when they are about to finish, they must be grand.
[Now, words are like wind and waves;
actions are like the loss of substance.
Wind and waves are easily stirred up,
and the loss of substance is easily endangered.
Therefore, anger is contrived without cause,
Cunning words and biased rhetoric.
When a beast is dying, it doesn't choose its cries.
Its breath is disordered,
and then resentment is born.
Being overly critical and exacting
will inevitably be met with a rebellious heart,
without knowing why.
If one truly doesn't know why,
who knows where it will end!
Therefore, the *Fǎ Yán* says:
"Don't change orders frequently,
don't urge completion,
excess is detrimental."
Changing orders and urging completion lead to failure.
Beautiful achievements take time.
Evils achieve completion too quickly to be corrected.
Shouldn't one be careful?
Moreover, to ride along with things to freely roam the mind,
relying on what cannot be helped to nurture the center,
is the ultimate.
Why act as if seeking recompense?
It is better to accept fate.
This is what is difficult."
Yán Hé was about to tutor the crown prince of Wèi Línggōng,
and asked Qú Bóyù, saying:
"There is a man here,
whose virtue is naturally destructive.
If I act with him without constraints,
Then it endangers our country.
If you deal with them with rigid principles,
then you endanger yourself.
Their knowledge is just enough to know others' faults,
but not enough to know the reason for their faults.
If that's the case, what can I do?"
Qū Bóyù said:
"Excellent question!
Be cautious of it, be careful of it,
and correct your own person!
In form, nothing is better than compliance;
in mind, nothing is better than harmony.
However,
these two have their problems.
Compliance should not become intrusive,
and harmony should not become expressive.
If compliance becomes intrusive,
it will lead to collapse and ruin,
to disintegration and failure.
If harmony becomes expressive,
it will lead to seeking fame and reputation,
to becoming monstrous and evil.
If they are like infants,
then also be like infants with them;
if they are without boundaries,
then also be without boundaries with them;
if they are without limits,
then also be without limits with them.
Dázhī,
you will enter a state of flawlessness.
Do you not know about the praying mantis?
It angrily raises its arms to stop a chariot wheel,
not knowing that it is incapable of the task.
This is an admirable quality of its talent.
Be warned, be cautious!
Those who accumulate achievements and consider themselves excellent will offend others because of it,
and they will be in danger.
Do you not know about those who raise tigers?
They dare not give them live animals,
for fear of enraging them when they kill;
they dare not give them whole animals,
for fear of enraging them when they tear them apart;
they monitor their hunger and satiety,
and understand their angry mood.
Though tigers and humans are different species,
they are tamed and nurtured because
they are compliant;
therefore, those they kill
are those who resist.
Now, those who love horses
use baskets to hold their droppings,
and shells to hold their urine.
If mosquitoes or gadflies land on them,
and one brushes them away at the wrong time,
it can break the bit, damage the head, and shatter the chest.
If the intention is there
If affection is directed towards something that can be lost,
how can one not be careful?"
The craftsman Shí
arrived in Qūyuán, Qí,
and saw a large oak tree at the local shrine.
Its size was enough to shade thousands of cattle,
and its circumference was a hundred spans.
Its height overlooked the mountain,
and branches only appeared after ten *rèn*.
The wood that could be obtained from its branches was enough for more than ten boats.
Onlookers were like a marketplace,
but the craftsman Bó did not even glance at it,
and continued walking without stopping.
His disciple, having gazed at it long enough,
hurried to catch up with the craftsman Shí,
and said:
"Since I have held an axe and followed you, Master,
I have never seen timber as beautiful as this.
Yet you, Master, are unwilling to look at it,
and continue walking without stopping,
why is that?"
The craftsman said:
"Enough,
say no more about it!
It is useless wood.
If made into a boat, it would sink;
if made into a coffin, it would quickly rot;
if made into a vessel, it would quickly break;
If it were used as a door, it would ooze sap;
if it were used as a pillar, it would be eaten by worms.
It is useless timber,
with nothing for which it can be used,
therefore it is able to be so long-lived."
Jiàng Shí returned,
and the lìshè (oak altar) appeared to him in a dream, saying:
"With what are you going to compare me?
Are you going to compare me to ornamented wood?
Now, the zā (crab apple), lí (pear), jú (tangerine), yòu (pomelo),
and fruits of the vine and gourd,
when their fruit is ripe, are stripped;
when stripped, they are disgraced.
The large branches are broken,
and the small branches are snapped off.
These use their ability
to embitter their lives,
therefore they do not complete their natural lifespan
and die prematurely,
bringing destruction upon themselves in the world.
Everything is like this.
Moreover, I have sought to be useless for a long time;
I nearly died,
but now I have obtained it,
making it greatly useful to me.
If I were useful,
would I have been able to attain this size?
Moreover, both you and I are things;
How can we understand its approach to judging things?
And this nearly dead, useless man,
how could he understand useless wood!"
Craftsman Shí awoke and examined his dream.
The disciple said:
"To seek out uselessness,
then why make it a shrine?"
He said:
"Keep it secret!
As if you hadn't spoken!
It is simply lodging there,
considering those who do not understand it as scolding and harsh.
If it weren't made into a shrine,
it would probably have been cut down!
Moreover, what it preserves is different from others,
and to praise it according to conventional standards,
is that not far off!"
Nánbó Zǐqí wandered in the mounds of Shāng,
and saw a great tree of unusual appearance,
so that a thousand four-horse carriages,
could be shaded beneath what it covered.
Zǐqí said:
"What tree is this?
Surely it must be a strange and special material!"
He looked up at its small branches,
and they were so twisted that they could not be used as beams;
He looked down at its large roots,
and they were split and unusable for coffins;
If one licks its leaves,
their mouth will fester and become wounded.
If one smells it,
it will make people delirious and drunk, not ceasing for three days.
Zǐ Qí said: "This fruit tree is useless,
and that's why it has grown so large.
Alas, the divine person considers it useless for this reason!"
In Sòng, there was a certain Jīng family
suitable for planting qiū (楸), bǎi (柏), and sāng (桑) trees.
Those with an armful or more in circumference,
the ones seeking stakes for monkey tethers cut them down.
Those with three or four armfuls in circumference,
the ones seeking fine material for high-ranking officials cut them down.
Those with seven or eight armfuls in circumference,
wealthy and rich families
seeking wood for coffins around tombs cut them down.
Therefore, they do not finish their natural lifespan,
but are cut down halfway by axes.
This is the trouble with being useful.
Therefore, those who
sacrifice a bull with a white forehead,
or a pig with a turned-up snout,
or people with hemorrhoids
should not cross the river.
The shamans and priests all know this,
because they are considered unlucky.
This is precisely why divine persons consider them very auspicious.
Zhīlí Shū,
with his chin hidden in his chest in Qí,
his shoulders higher than his head,
his queue gathered pointing to the sky,
his five vital organs on top,
and his two thighs as ribs.
Mending with needles and removing knots,
he was able to support himself.
Playing with counting sticks and spreading his knowledge,
he was able to feed ten people.
When the ruler levied soldiers,
Zhīlí pushed his way through the crowd with raised arms.
When there was a major corvée labor,
Zhīlí, because of his chronic illness, did not receive the labor assignment.
When the ruler distributed grain to the sick,
he received three *zhōng* of grain and ten bundles of firewood.
Even one deformed in body like Zhīlí
is still able to nourish himself
and finish out his natural lifespan.
How much more so, then, one deformed in virtue!
Kǒngzǐ went to Chǔ,
and the madman Jiē Yú of Chǔ roamed by his gate, saying:
"Phoenix, O phoenix,
what a decline of virtue!
The coming age cannot be waited for,
the past age cannot be pursued.
When the world is well-ordered,
sages succeed;
When the world lacks the Way,
sages are born.
In these present times,
one can barely avoid punishment.
Blessings are lighter than feathers,
and no one knows how to carry them;
misfortune is heavier than the earth,
and no one knows how to avoid it.
Enough, enough!
Govern people with virtue!
Perilous, perilous!
Drawing lines on the ground and hurrying along them!
Dim light, dim light,
do not harm my journey!
Crooked path, crooked path,
do not injure my feet!"
Trees in the mountains invite their own destruction;
grease in a lamp invites its own burning.
Cinnamon is edible,
therefore it is cut down;
lacquer is useful,
therefore it is tapped.
Everyone knows the usefulness of the useful,
but no one knows the usefulness of the useless.
Chapter 5: Dé Chōng Fú (Inward Power Fully Realized)
In Lǔ, there was a cripple named Wáng Tái
and those who followed and studied with him
comparable to Zhòng Ní 仲尼.
Cháng Jì 常季 asked Zhòng Ní 仲尼, saying:
"Wáng Tái 王駘 is a mutilated man.
Those who follow him divide Lǔ 魯 equally with you, Master.
He stands without teaching,
he sits without discussing.
They go to him empty,
and return full.
Does he truly have instruction without words,
and form hearts without physical form?
What kind of person is this?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"That man is a sage.
I, Qiū 丘, have only been behind him and have not yet gone to him.
I will take him as my teacher,
how much more so those who are not as good as I!
What need is there to borrow the state of Lǔ 魯!
I will draw the whole world and follow him."
Cháng Jì 常季 said:
"He is a mutilated man,
yet he surpasses you as a teacher.
He is far removed from ordinary people.
If this is the case,
how is his mind uniquely employed?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"Life and death are indeed great,
yet he does not change with them.
Even if heaven and earth were to overturn and collapse,
and also will not leave anything behind for them.
Clearly understanding that there is nothing false and not changing with things,
ordering the transformation of things,
and guarding their source."
Cháng Jì 常季 said:
"What does this mean?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"If you look at them from their differences,
the liver and gallbladder are like Chǔ 楚 and Yuè 越;
if you look at them from their sameness,
all things are one.
If it is like that, then one will not know what the ears and eyes are suited for,
and will roam the mind in the harmony of virtue;
one sees things as being one
and does not see what is lost,
seeing the loss of one's foot is like losing a clod of earth."
Cháng Jì 常季 said:
"He acts for himself, using his knowledge
to obtain his heart, and using his heart
to obtain his constant heart,
why would things bother him?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"People do not look at flowing water for a reflection,
but look at still water,
only stillness can still all stillness.
Receiving its mandate from the earth,
only pine and cypress are unique
in being green in winter and summer;
Receiving the mandate from Heaven,
Only Shùn 舜 was truly upright.
Fortunate to be born upright,
He used his uprightness to rectify all living beings.
The sign of preserving the beginning lies in the reality of not fearing.
A brave warrior, alone, valiantly enters nine armies.
If a general seeks fame and can restrain himself, and still does this,
How much more so one who governs Heaven and Earth,
Embraces the myriad things,
Merely dwells in his six physical components,
Uses his ears and eyes to perceive what is knowable,
And whose heart has never died?
He will choose a day to ascend,
And people will follow him.
How could he possibly be willing to be occupied with external things?"
Shēntú Jiā 申徒嘉 was a mutilated man,
And studied under Bó Hūn Wúrén 伯昏无人 with Zhèng Zǐchǎn 郑子产.
Zǐchǎn 郑子产 said to Shēntú Jiā 申徒嘉:
"If I exit first, then you stay;
If you exit first, then I stay."
The next day, they again sat together in the same hall and on the same mat.
Zǐchǎn 郑子产 said to Shēntú Jiā 申徒嘉:
"If I exit first, then you stay;
If you exit first, then I stay.
Now I am about to exit,
Can you stay, or not yet?
Moreover, you see the one in power
And do not avoid him.
Zǐ Qí is in power, isn't he?"
Shēntú Jiā said:
"Among the disciples of our teacher,
how can there be someone who holds power in such a way?
Are you praising Zǐ’s governance
by belittling others?
I have heard it said:
'If a mirror is clear, then dust will not settle on it;
if dust settles, then it will not be clear.
To associate with virtuous people for a long time will prevent errors.'
Now, the greatest thing you have received is our teacher,
and yet you still speak such words;
is this not also an error?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"Since you are like this,
you still compete with Yáo in goodness.
Considering your virtue,
is it sufficient for self-reflection?"
Shēntú Jiā said:
"Many are those who describe their faults
as not deserving death,
and few are those who do not describe their faults
as not deserving to live.
To know that something cannot be helped
and to accept it as fate,
only the virtuous are capable of this.
Imagine walking within the range of Yì's bow.
The center is the easiest place to hit;
However, failing is a matter of fate.
Many people laugh at me for being incomplete, while they are complete;
I was indignantly angry.
But upon going to Xiānshēng's 先生 place,
I returned dejected.
I wonder if Xiānshēng 先生 is cleansing me with goodness?
I have been traveling with Fūzǐ 夫子 for nineteen years,
and I have never known that I was a stump.
Now you travel with me within the confines of our physical forms,
yet you seek me outside the confines of our physical forms.
Isn't that going too far!"
Zǐchǎn 子產 changed his expression abruptly
and said with a changed countenance:
"Please, don't say that!"
In Lǔ 魯, there was a stump, Shūshān Wúzhǐ 叔山无趾,
who went to see Zhòngní 仲尼.
Zhòngní 仲尼 said, "You were not careful,
and you previously committed an offense and suffered such a misfortune.
Even if you come now, what good is it?"
Wúzhǐ 无趾 said:
"I only failed to be cautious and lightly used my body,
which is why I lost my feet.
Now I have come,
because there is still something more valuable than feet that exists,
and I am determined to preserve it completely.
Heaven covers everything,
and Earth supports everything.
I regard Fūzǐ 夫子 as Heaven and Earth.
How could I have known that the Master was like this!"
Kǒngzǐ said, "I, Qiū, am indeed ignorant.
Why doesn't the Master come in?
Please, let me explain what I have heard!"
Wúzhǐ went out.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Disciples, strive!
This Wúzhǐ, is a mutilated man,
yet he still strives to learn
in order to remedy the wrong of his past actions,
how much more should a person of complete virtue!"
Wúzhǐ said to Lǎodān,
"Kǒng Qiū's understanding of the perfect man,
is it not lacking?
Why is he so respectful in learning from you?
He is merely seeking fame through strange and deceptive names,
not knowing that the perfect man considers these things to be shackles."
Lǎodān said,
"Why not directly make him regard life and death as a single thread,
and consider acceptable and unacceptable as a single principle,
to loosen his shackles, would that be possible?"
Wúzhǐ said,
"Heaven has punished him, how can he be freed!"
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Zhòngní,
"In Wèi there is an ugly man, named Āi Dài Tuó.
The men who associate with him,
think of him and cannot bear to leave him.
Women who see him plead with their parents, saying,
"Rather be a concubine to a teacher than a wife to another man,"
has been said dozens of times and hasn't stopped.
I have never heard anyone initiate such a sentiment;
they always merely echo others.
I have no position as a ruler
to relieve people from death,
nor do I amass wealth to satisfy people's bellies.
Moreover, she startles the world with her ugliness,
echoes but does not initiate,
and her knowledge does not extend beyond her immediate surroundings.
Furthermore, male and female are coupled before her.
She must be different from others.
I summoned her to observe her,
and indeed, she startled the world with her ugliness.
After being with me for less than a month,
I became interested in her character.
Before a year had passed,
I trusted her.
As the state had no chancellor,
I entrusted the state to her.
She responded with hesitation,
and broadly refused.
Ashamed as I was,
I ultimately gave her the state.
Before long, she left me and departed.
I was saddened by it, as if I had lost something,
as if there was no joy in ruling the state without her.
What kind of person is she?"
Zhòng Ní said:
"Qiū once served as an envoy to Chǔ.
I happened to see piglets
eating their dead mother.
Shortly after, they blinked and all abandoned her and ran away.
Once she could no longer be seen,
they could no longer relate to her.
What they loved about their mother
was not her form,
but what made her form function.
Those who die in battle,
when those people are buried,
they are not provided with feather fans as grave goods;
the shoes of a amputee,
there is no reason to cherish them;
both have lost their essence.
The imperial concubines of the Son of Heaven,
do not clip their nails,
do not pierce their ears;
those who marry the empress stop serving outside,
and are not allowed to serve again.
Preserving the physical form is still enough for this,
how much more so for a person of complete virtue!
Now, Āi Dài Tuó, without speaking, is trusted,
without accomplishment, is intimate,
causing people to offer him their state,
only fearing that he will not accept it,
he must be one whose talent is complete but whose virtue is not outwardly displayed."
Āi Gōng said, "What is meant by 'complete talent'?"
Zhòng Ní said:
"Life and death, survival and extinction,
poverty and success, wealth and destitution,
being worthy or unworthy, defamation and praise,
hunger, thirst, cold, and heat—
these are the changes of events,
the workings of fate.
Day and night alternate before us,
yet our knowledge cannot predict their beginning.
Therefore, these are not enough to disturb harmony,
nor can they enter the spiritual abode.
Cause them to be harmonious and joyful,
thorough without being lost in pleasure.
Make day and night seamless,
and be in spring with all things.
This is connecting and generating the seasons in one’s heart.
This is what is meant by 'complete talent.'"
"[What is meant by] 'virtue without form'?"
He said:
"Levelness is the height of still water.
It can be a standard,
preserving it internally while not being swayed externally.
Virtue is the cultivated achievement of harmony.
Virtue without form means
that things cannot leave it."
On another day, Āi Gōng told Mǐn Zǐ,
"At first, I used my position facing south
"Ruling the world,
grasping the reins of the people,
and yet being worried about their deaths,
I considered myself to have attained perfect understanding.
But now I have heard the words of a perfect man,
and I fear that I am without substance,
lightly using my body and destroying my country.
My relationship with Kǒng Qiū 孔丘 is not that of ruler and subject,
but merely that of friends based on virtue."
Yīn Qǐ 闉跂, a cripple without a calf, persuaded Wèi Línggōng 衛靈公,
and Línggōng 靈公 was pleased with him;
but when he looked at complete men,
their necks seemed scrawny.
Wèng Àng 甕盎, a man with a large goiter, persuaded Qí Huángōng 齊桓公,
and Huángōng 桓公 was pleased with him;
but when he looked at complete men,
their necks seemed scrawny.
Therefore, when virtue excels in one aspect,
form is forgotten in another.
If people do not forget what they should forget,
and forget what they should not forget,
this is called true forgetting.
Therefore, the sage has his wanderings,
and considers knowledge to be a misfortune,
covenants to be glue,
virtue to be a means of connection,
and skill to be a form of commerce.
The sage does not scheme,
How would one know how to use an adze?
If one does not chop,
how would one use glue?
If there is no loss,
how would one use virtue?
If one does not trade,
how would one use merchants?
These four,
are nurtured by Heaven.
To be nurtured by Heaven,
is to be fed by Heaven.
Since one has already received sustenance from Heaven,
what need is there to use man!
One has the form of a man,
but not the emotions of a man.
Because one has the form of a man,
therefore one groups with men;
because one does not have the emotions of a man,
therefore right and wrong do not affect one personally.
How small indeed
is that which belongs to man!
How great indeed
is being alone to complete one’s Heaven!
Huìzi said to Zhuāngzi:
"Do men truly have no emotions?"
Zhuāngzi said:
"Yes."
Huìzi said:
"If a person is without emotions,
how can he be called a person?"
Zhuāng Zǐ said:
"The Dào gives him his appearance,
Heaven gives him his form,
how can one not call him a person?"
Huìzi said:
"Since he is called a person,
how can he be without emotions?"
Zhuāng Zǐ said:
"This is not what I mean by emotions.
What I mean by being without emotions
is that a person does not inwardly harm his body with likes and dislikes,
but constantly relies on nature and does not increase life."
Huìzi said:
"If he does not increase life,
how can he possess his body?"
Zhuāng Zǐ said:
"The Dào gives him his appearance,
Heaven gives him his form,
and he does not inwardly harm his body with likes and dislikes.
Now, you are external to your spirit,
exhausting your essence,
leaning against a tree and chanting,
leaning on a withered *wútóng* tree and closing your eyes.
Heaven selected your form,
and you proclaim your arguments on hardness and whiteness!"
The Great and Venerable Teacher, Chapter Six
To know what Heaven does,
and to know what man does,
is perfection.
To know what Heaven does
is to be born of Heaven.
To know what man does
is to use one’s knowing of the known
to nourish one’s knowing of the unknown,
to complete one's natural lifespan
without dying prematurely in the middle of the road—
this is the height of knowledge.
However, there is still trouble.
For knowledge must rely on something before it is appropriate,
but what it relies on is not yet determined.
How can we know that what I call Heaven is not really man?
Or that what I call man is not really Heaven?
Only after there is a True Person is there True Knowledge.
What is a True Person?
The True Persons of old
did not oppose scarcity,
did not pride themselves on success,
and did not scheme against officers.
Such a person,
even if he errs, does not regret it;
even if he is right, he does not congratulate himself.
Such a person,
ascends to great heights without trembling,
Entering water, they are not wetted;
entering fire, they are not burned.
From this we know that knowledge can ascend and rely on the Dao to such an extent.
The true people of old,
when they slept, did not dream;
when they awoke, they had no worries;
when they ate, they did not crave delicacies;
their breathing was deep.
The breathing of true people is from their heels;
the breathing of ordinary people is from their throats.
Those who are subjugated and compliant,
their throat sounds are like retching.
Those whose desires are deep,
their heavenly mechanism is shallow.
The true people of old
did not rejoice in being born,
did not abhor death;
their departure was not a cause for joy,
their arrival was not a cause for resistance;
they went away freely,
they came back freely
and that was all.
They did not remember where they began,
they did not seek where they would end;
they accepted and rejoiced in it,
they forgot it and returned to it;
this is what is called
Do not abandon the Dao with the mind,
do not assist Heaven with human effort.
This is what is called a True Person (Zhēn Rén).
Those who are like this,
their minds forget,
their appearance is still,
their foreheads are broad;
they are melancholic like autumn,
warm like spring,
joy and anger accord with the four seasons,
and their dealings with things are appropriate
yet no one knows their limit.
Therefore, when the sage uses the military,
he loses the state but does not lose the people's hearts;
he bestows benefits on myriad generations,
but does not do it out of love for others.
Therefore, to delight in conforming to things
is not the way of the sage;
to have attachments
is not benevolence;
to be bound by seasonal timing
is not wisdom;
to be unable to discern benefit and harm
is not the way of the gentleman;
to sacrifice oneself for fame and lose oneself
is not the way of the scholar;
to lose oneself and not be genuine
is not the way of the servant of others.
Ruò Húbùxié, Wù Guāng, Bó Yí, Shū Qí, Jī Zǐ, Xū Yú, Jì Tā, Shēntú Dí,
these are those who labor at others' labor,
and find comfort in others' comfort,
and do not find their own comfort in their own comfort.
The perfected persons of old,
their demeanor was righteous but they did not form cliques;
as if lacking, yet they did not fawn;
with their angularity, they were not rigid;
extended in their emptiness, they were not flowery;
radiant, they seemed joyful!
Overwhelmed, as if they could not help themselves!
Overflowing, their faces advanced towards me,
and with their virtues they stopped me;
stern, they seemed worldly!
Untamed, they were beyond control;
continuous, they seemed fond of seclusion;
oblivious, they forgot their words.
They took punishment as their body,
ritual as their wings,
knowledge as their timing,
and virtue as their guidance.
Taking punishment as their body
meant being exceedingly lethal;
taking ritual as their wings
was how they moved in the world;
taking knowledge as their timing
was how they could not help but be involved in affairs;
To follow virtue as a guide,
it is said that even a person with sufficient feet can only reach a mound (hill);
yet people truly consider them diligent travelers.
Therefore, what they like is unified,
and what they dislike is unified.
Their unity is unified,
and their non-unity is unified.
Their unity is a companion with Heaven,
their non-unity is a companion with humanity.
Heaven and humanity do not overcome each other,
this is what is called a True Person (zhēn rén).
Death and life are destiny;
their having the constancy of night and day is
Heaven.
What humans cannot obtain together with them
are all the inherent natures of things.
They especially take Heaven as their father
and yet still love their own body;
how much more so that which is outstanding!
People especially consider having a ruler better than themselves,
and yet still die for him;
how much more so that which is genuine!
When a spring dries up,
fish are together on land,
panting moist breath at each other,
and moistening each other with foam;
it is better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes.
Rather than praising Yáo 堯 and criticizing Jié 桀,
it is better to forget both
and be transformed by their Dao.
Now, the Great Clod (Nature) burdens me with form,
toils me with life,
eases me with old age,
and rests me with death.
Therefore, to cherish my life
is precisely to cherish my death.
Now, to hide a boat in a ravine
or a mountain in a swamp
is considered secure.
Yet, in the middle of the night, a strong man might carry it away,
and the foolish would not know.
Hiding small things and large things each has its proper place,
yet there is still a way to escape.
But to hide the universe in the universe
and find no way to escape,
that is the great reality of constant things.
To temporarily possess the form of a human
and yet rejoice in it—
the form of a human
undergoes ten thousand transformations and has never had a beginning or end.
How can the joy of that be fully reckoned!
Therefore, the sage will wander in that in which things cannot escape and all exist.
He cherishes premature death and old age,
cherishes beginning and end.
People still emulate him;
Moreover, it is that upon which all things depend,
and by which the single transformation is awaited!
Now, the Dao,
possesses both emotion and trustworthiness,
is without action and without form;
it can be transmitted but not received,
it can be attained but not seen;
from root and from source,
before there were Heaven and Earth,
it existed firmly since ancient times;
it spiritualizes ghosts and spiritualizes emperors,
it gives birth to Heaven and gives birth to Earth;
it is prior to the Great Ultimate, yet does not consider itself to be high,
it is below the Six Extremes, yet does not consider itself to be deep,
it was born before Heaven and Earth, yet does not consider itself to be old,
it is longer than high antiquity, yet does not consider itself to be aged.
Xī Wěi Shì obtained it,
and with it, held together Heaven and Earth;
Fú Xī obtained it,
and with it, perpetuated the breath-mother;
Wéi Dǒu obtained it,
and to the end of time does not err;
the sun and moon obtained it,
and to the end of time do not cease;
Kān Huài obtained it,
and with it, perpetuated the Kūnlún Mountains;
Féng Yí obtained it,
and with it, roamed the great rivers;
Jiān Wú obtained it,
and dwelt in the great mountains;
Huángdì obtained it,
and ascended the cloudy heavens;
Zhuānxū obtained it,
and dwelt in the mysterious palace;
Yú Qiáng obtained it,
and stood at the North Pole;
Xī Wángmǔ obtained it,
and sat upon Shǎo Guǎng,
no one knows its beginning,
no one knows its end;
Péng Zǔ obtained it,
reaching back to Yǒu Yú,
and down to the Five Hegemons;
Fù Yuè obtained it,
and became the minister of Wǔ Dīng,
possessing all under Heaven,
riding the Eastern Cord,
astride the Dipper and Tail,
and ranked among the stars.
Nánbó Zǐ Kuí asked Nǚ Yǔ, saying:
"Your years are advanced,
yet your complexion is like that of a child,
why is this?"
He said:
"I have heard the Dao."
Nánbó Zǐkuí said, "Can the Dao be learned?"
He replied:
"Alas! How can it be?
You are not the right person.
Now, Bǔ Liángyǐ has the talent of a sage
but lacks the Dao of a sage.
I have the Dao of a sage
but lack the talent of a sage.
I wanted to teach him,
hoping that he might truly become a sage!
If not, it would be easy to impart the Dao of a sage to the talent of a sage.
I still guarded him and told him about it.
After three days, he was able to disregard the world.
Having disregarded the world,
I guarded him again.
After seven days, he was able to disregard things.
Having disregarded things,
I guarded him again.
After nine days, he was able to disregard life.
Having disregarded life,
then he was able to attain morning clarity.
With morning clarity,
then he was able to perceive the Alone.
Perceiving the Alone,
then he was able to transcend past and present.
Transcending past and present,
then he was able to enter into non-death and non-birth.
He who kills life does not die;
That which generates life is not itself alive.
As a thing,
there is nothing it does not send away,
nothing it does not welcome;
nothing it does not destroy,
nothing it does not complete.
Its name is called Yīngníng.
Yīngníng is
that which is formed after being disturbed."
Nánbó Zǐkuí said:
"From where did you alone hear this?"
He said:
"I heard it from the son of Fùmò,
the son of Fùmò heard it from the grandson of Luòsòng,
the grandson of Luòsòng heard it from Zhānmíng,
Zhānmíng heard it from Nièxǔ,
Nièxǔ heard it from Xūyì,
Xūyì heard it from Yūōu,
Yūōu heard it from Xuánmíng,
Xuánmíng heard it from Cānliáo,
Cānliáo heard it from Yíshǐ."
Zǐsì, Zǐyú, Zǐlí, and Zǐlái,
four men, spoke together, saying:
"Who can take non-being as the head,
life as the spine,
and death as the tailbone?
Who knows that life, death, existence, and destruction are one and the same?
"I will be friends with him."
The four men looked at each other and smiled,
understanding each other deeply in their hearts,
and so they became friends.
Soon after, Zǐ Yú (子輿) fell ill,
and Zǐ Sì (子祀) went to visit him.
Zǐ Yú (子輿) said, "Great indeed is the Creator! Is he about to make me into this hunched-up form?
My back is hunched and my spine protrudes,
my five organs are above,
my chin is hidden by my navel,
my shoulders are higher than my head,
and my neck points towards the sky."
The Yin and Yang energies are in disharmony,
but my heart is at peace and without concern.
I hobble to the well and look at my reflection,
and I say:
"Alas!
Is the Creator again about to make me into this hunched-up form!"
Zǐ Sì (子祀) said, "Do you dislike it?"
Zǐ Yú (子輿) said:
"No, why should I dislike it!
If, gradually, he were to transform my left arm
into a rooster,
I would use it to tell the time at night;
if, gradually, he were to transform my right arm
into a pellet,
I would use it to roast an owl;
jìn jiǎ ér huà yǔ zhī kāo yǐ wéi lún,
and my spirit into a horse.
I will then ride it.
Why would I need to change carriages again?
Moreover, obtaining is a matter of timing;
losing is a matter of accordance.
Being at peace with timing and dwelling in accordance,
sorrow and joy cannot enter.
This is what the ancients called being released from bonds,
but those who cannot release themselves
have things binding them.
Moreover, things have not overcome Heaven
for a long time.
What is there for me to hate?"
Soon after, Zǐ Lái fell ill,
panting and on the verge of death.
His wife and children surrounded him and wept.
Lí went to ask about him,
saying:
"Shoo! Step aside! Do not startle the transformation!"
Leaning against the door, he spoke to him, saying:
"Great is the Creator!
What will it use you for again?
Where will it send you?
Will it make you into a rat's liver?
Will it make you into an insect's arm?"
Zǐ Lái said:
"Parents to their children,
To the east, west, north, and south,
I obey its commands.
Yin and yang to man
are no less than parents;
if it approaches my death
and I do not listen,
then I am violent and rebellious,
but what fault is it of theirs?
Now, the great earth carries me with form,
exhausts me with life,
eases me with old age,
and rests me with death.
Therefore, to cherish my life
is precisely how to cherish my death.
Now, if a great smelter casts metal,
and the metal leaps up and says,
"I must surely become Mòyé!"
the great smelter will certainly consider it an inauspicious metal.
Now, having once assumed the form of a man,
to say "A man! A man!"
the creator will certainly consider him an inauspicious man.
Now, if one considers Heaven and Earth as a great furnace,
and the Creator as a great smelter,
where can one go that is not possible!"
Chéng Rán fell asleep,
and suddenly awoke.
Zǐ Sānghù, Mèng Zǐfǎn, and Zǐ Qínzhāng, three men who were friends, said:
"Who can associate with one another in non-association,
and act for one another in non-action?
Who can ascend to the heavens and wander in the mists,
twist and turn in the limitless?
Forgetting each other in life, with no end to exhaustion?"
The three men looked at each other and laughed,
finding a mutual understanding in their hearts,
and thus became friends.
After a while, quietly,
Zǐsāng Hù died,
and had not yet been buried.
Kǒngzǐ heard of it
and sent Zǐgòng to attend to the affairs.
One was arranging music,
another was playing the zither,
harmonizing and singing, saying:
"Alas, Zīsāng Hù!
Alas, Zīsāng Hù!
He has returned to his true self,
while I am still clinging to human form!"
Zǐgòng hurried forward and said:
"May I ask,
is it proper to sing beside a corpse?"
The two men looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"How could he possibly understand the meaning of ritual!"
Zǐgòng returned
and told Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"What sort of people are they?
He has no cultivation,
yet he disregards his physical form.
He sings beside a corpse, his expression unchanged.
I don't know what to call it.
What kind of person is he?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"That is someone who wanders beyond the square;
and I, Qiū, am someone who wanders within the square.
The outer and inner do not interact,
and that I, Qiū, would have you go to offer condolences to him, would be a sign of my own narrowness.
He is about to make the Creator his companion,
and wanders in the single breath of Heaven and Earth.
He regards life as an attached goiter or protruding wart,
and death as the bursting of a boil or the draining of a tumor.
Someone like that,
how could he possibly know where life and death, before and after, lie?
He borrows from different things,
entrusts himself to the same body.
He forgets his liver and gall bladder,
abandons his ears and eyes.
Reversing back and forth, beginning and end,
he does not know the slightest clue.
He wanders blankly outside the dust and dirt,
leisurely in the business of non-action.
How could he possibly be muddled by the rituals of the world,
to watch the ears and eyes of the crowd!"
Zǐgòng said:
"Then what way does the Master rely on?"
He said:
"Qiū, I am a condemned person of Heaven.
Nevertheless, I will share it with you."
Zǐgòng said: "May I venture to ask the method?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Fish find mutual benefit in water,
people find mutual benefit in the Dao.
Those who find mutual benefit in water
dig ponds and maintain a sufficient supply;
those who find mutual benefit in the Dao
without effort find life settled.
Therefore, it is said,
fish forget each other in rivers and lakes,
people forget each other in the Dao and techniques."
Zǐgòng said:
"May I venture to ask about the 'eccentric person' (jī rén)?"
He said:
"The 'eccentric person' (jī rén)
is eccentric in relation to people but corresponds to Heaven.
Therefore, it is said:
a petty person of Heaven
is a superior person of people;
a superior person of people
is a petty person of Heaven."
Yānhuí asked Zhòngní, saying:
"Mèngsūn is talented,
but when his mother died,
he wept without tears,
His center is not sorrowful;
in mourning, he is not grieving.
Without these three things,
he used a "good" funeral to cover up the state of Lǔ.
Could there be someone who inherently lacks the reality but obtains the name?
Huí completely doubts this."
Zhòng Ní said:
"Mèng Sūnshì has exhausted this;
he has advanced to knowledge.
It's just that he simplifies it
and cannot grasp it completely,
but he has already simplified something.
Mèng Sūnshì
does not know the reason for living,
does not know the reason for dying;
does not know to go before,
does not know to go after;
as if transforming into a thing,
awaiting the transformation of what he does not know!
Moreover, when about to transform,
how can he know that he will not transform?
When about not to transform,
how can he know that he has already transformed?
I, especially with you,
are perhaps those whose dream has not yet begun to awaken!
Furthermore, he has a frightening appearance
but no damage to his heart,
has a morning abode
and die without feeling.
When Mèngsūn Shì particularly becomes aware,
he cries when others cry;
this is acting out of what causes it.
Moreover, we are mutually lending our ears,
how can we know that what I call "I" is truly "I"?
Furthermore, you dream of being a bird and soaring in the sky,
dream of being a fish and sinking into the depths.
Do you not know that those who speak now,
are they awake,
or are they dreaming?
Rushing towards pleasure, one does not have time to laugh;
offering laughter, one does not have time to arrange it;
arranging and departing from transformation
is to enter into the vast unity of Heaven."
Yìérzi went to see Xǔ Yóu.
Xǔ Yóu said:
"How did Yáo assist you?"
Yìérzi said:
"Yáo told me:
'You must personally practice benevolence and righteousness
and clearly speak about right and wrong.'"
Xǔ Yóu said: "Why have you come to Zhǐ?
Yáo has already tattooed you with benevolence and righteousness,
and cut off your nose with right and wrong,
how will you wander the path of unfettered, unrestrained, and shifting wanderings?"
Yìérzi said: "Even so,
I wish to wander in its confines."
Xǔ Yóu said, "Not so.
A blind person cannot appreciate the beauty of eyebrows and eyes,
and a blind musician cannot appreciate the sight of green and yellow embroidered patterns."
Yì Érzi said,
"That Wú Zhuāng lost his beauty,
that Jù Liáng lost his strength,
that Huángdì lost his wisdom,
all happened in the process of being forged and hammered.
How do you know that the Creator will not cease to mark me with tattoos and heal my mutilated nose,
so that I can ride in a carriage to follow you, Master?"
Xǔ Yóu said, "Alas! It cannot be known.
I will tell you its general outline.
My teacher! My teacher!
He hammers and shapes all things
without considering it righteous,
his beneficence extends to myriad generations
without considering it benevolent,
he is older than the ancient past
without considering himself old,
he covers and carries heaven and earth,
carves and shapes the myriad forms,
without considering it skillful.
This is where he roams."
Yán Huí said,
"I have progressed."
Zhòng Ní said,
"What do you mean?"
He said,
"[Huí] has forgotten rites and music."
The master said,
"That's acceptable,
but still not quite there."
Another day, he saw him again,
and said, "[Huí] has improved."
The master said,
"What do you mean?"
[Huí] said,
"[Huí] has forgotten benevolence and righteousness."
The master said,
"That's acceptable, but still not quite there."
Another day, he saw him again, and said, "[Huí] has improved."
The master said,
"What do you mean?"
[Huí] said,
"[Huí] has achieved sitting in forgetfulness."
Zhòng Ní abruptly straightened up and said,
"What is sitting in forgetfulness?"
Yán Huí said,
"To cast off my limbs,
banish my intelligence,
separate from form and cast off knowledge,
to be one with the Great Thoroughfare,
this is what is called sitting in forgetfulness."
Zhòng Ní said,
"To be the same is to have no preference,
to transform is to have no constancy.
And indeed, is he virtuous?
Qiū, may I ask to follow behind him."
Zǐyú was friends with Zǐsāng,
and there was ten days of continuous rain.
Zǐyú said:
"Zǐsāng is probably ill!"
He wrapped rice and went to feed him.
Arriving at Zǐsāng's door,
he was as if singing, as if crying,
playing the qin, saying:
"Father!
Mother!
Heaven!
Man!"
There was a straining of his voice
and a rushing to recite his poem.
Zǐyú entered and said:
"Your singing poem,
why is it like this?"
He said:
"I ponder upon that which has caused me to reach this extremity
but cannot find it.
Did my parents desire my poverty?
Heaven has no private covering,
Earth has no private bearing,
would Heaven and Earth privately impoverish me?
I seek one who did it
but cannot find him.
And yet, that I have reached this extremity,
he transforms and lends to all things
yet the people do not rely on him;
his name is never brought up,
he causes things to delight in themselves;
he abides in the unfathomable,
and wanders in the realm of nothingness."
In Zhèng there was a divine shaman
named Jì Xián,
who knew men's death, existence, survival, and ruin,
misfortune, fortune, longevity, and premature death,
predicting them with the certainty of years, months, and days,
as if he were a god.
The people of Zhèng, upon seeing him,
all abandoned their tasks and fled.
Lièzǐ, upon seeing him, was captivated,
and upon returning home, told Húzi, saying,
"At first, I considered my master's (Húzi's) Dao to be the ultimate,
but now there is one who has surpassed it."
Húzi said,
"I have only given you the outward form of the Dao,
and have not yet given you its substance.
Do you really think you have grasped the Dao?
So, what is the need for Rén 仁 and Yì 義
to be constantly like glue, lacquer, and ropes,
and to wander between morality and virtue,
causing the world to be confused!
Small confusion changes direction;
great confusion changes nature.
How do we know that this is so?
Since the Yú 虞 clan summoned Rén 仁 and Yì 義 to stir up the world,
everyone under Heaven has been rushing around for Rén 仁 and Yì 義.
Is it not that they are changing their nature with Rén 仁 and Yì 義?
Therefore, let us try to discuss it.
From the Three Dynasties onwards,
everyone under Heaven has exchanged their nature for things.
Petty people sacrifice themselves for profit;
scholars sacrifice themselves for fame;
high officials sacrifice themselves for their families;
sages sacrifice themselves for the world.
Therefore, these several people,
Their occupations are different,
and their reputations and titles vary,
but in harming their nature and sacrificing their lives,
they are the same.
Zāng and Gǔ, two men
who together herded sheep and both lost their sheep.
If you ask Zāng what he was doing,
he was holding a tally counter and reading books;
if you ask Gǔ what he was doing,
he was playing the game of bó sè (a type of board game) for amusement.
These two men, their occupations are different,
but in losing their sheep, they are the same.
Bó Yí died seeking fame at the foot of Mount Shǒuyáng,
and Dào Zhí died seeking profit on top of the Eastern Mound.
These two men, what they died for is different,
but in damaging their lives and harming their nature,
they are the same.
Why must we say Bó Yí is right and Dào Zhí is wrong?
The whole world is devoted to something.
If they devote themselves to benevolence and righteousness,
then the common people call them gentlemen;
if they devote themselves to wealth and possessions,
then the common people call them petty men.
Their devotion is the same,
yet there are gentlemen,
and there are petty men.
If it comes to damaging life and harming nature,
then Dào Zhí is also Bó Yí,
How then can one distinguish between the junzi (君子, gentleman) and the xiaoren (小人, petty person) in such matters?
Moreover, those whose nature is aligned with benevolence and righteousness,
even if they are as well-versed as Zēng Shēn (曾參) and Shǐ Yú (史鰌),
are not what I consider to be good.
Those whose nature is aligned with the five flavors,
even if they are as well-versed as Yú Ér (俞兒),
are not what I consider to be good.
Those whose nature is aligned with the five sounds,
even if they are as well-versed as Shī Kuàng (師曠),
are not what I consider to be perceptive.
Those whose nature is aligned with the five colors,
even if they are as well-versed as Lí Zhū (離朱),
are not what I consider to be clear-sighted.
What I consider good is not about benevolence and righteousness;
it is simply being good in one's own virtue.
What I consider good
is not about so-called benevolence and righteousness;
it is simply following the natural feelings of one's own nature and destiny.
What I consider perceptive
is not about hearing others;
it is simply hearing oneself.
What I consider clear-sighted
is not about seeing others;
it is simply seeing oneself.
To see others without seeing oneself,
to gain from others without gaining from oneself,
is to gain what others gain
without gaining one's own gain.
適人之適
and does not conform to what is natural to themselves.
If one conforms to what others conform to
and does not conform to what is natural to themselves,
even if it's Dào Zhí and Bó Yí,
they are equally being excessive and eccentric.
I am ashamed with regards to morality,
therefore above I dare not engage in acts of benevolence and righteousness,
and below I dare not engage in excessive and eccentric behavior.
Horses' hooves can tread on frost and snow,
their fur can ward off wind and cold,
they graze on grass and drink water,
they lift their feet and leap across the land;
this is the true nature of horses.
Even if there are lofty platforms and luxurious chambers,
they are of no use to them.
When Bó Lè arrived,
he said, "I am good at managing horses."
He singed them,
trimmed them,
carved them,
branded them,
connected them with reins and halters,
confined them to dark stables;
of the horses, twelve or thirteen out of ten died.
He made them hungry,
They made them thirsty,
drove them fast,
rushed them onward,
disciplined them,
aligned them,
with the threat of ornamental posts ahead,
and the intimidation of whips and goads behind,
and more than half the horses died.
A potter said:
"I am good at working with clay,
round things hit the compass,
square things hit the square."
A craftsman said:
"I am good at working with wood,
curved things hit the hook,
straight things accord with the plumb line."
But the nature of clay and wood,
how could they desire to hit the compass, square, hook, and plumb line?
Yet generation after generation calls them:
"Bólè is good at managing horses,
and potters and craftsmen are good at managing clay and wood."
This is also the fault of those who govern the world.
My opinion is that those who are good at governing the world are not like this.
The people have a constant nature:
they weave to make clothes,
they plow to obtain food;
this is called sharing virtue;
being unified without forming factions,
This is called letting nature take its course (tiān fàng).
Therefore, in the age of supreme virtue,
their actions were simple and steady (tián tián),
their gaze was unfocused and natural (diān diān).
At that time,
mountains had no paths or tunnels,
marshes had no boats or bridges;
the myriad things lived together,
connected to their habitats;
birds and beasts formed groups,
grasses and trees grew freely.
Therefore, birds and beasts could be tethered and led for amusement,
and the nests of magpies could be climbed and peered into.
In the age of supreme virtue,
people lived together with birds and beasts,
belonged to the same kin as the myriad things,
how would they know the difference between the noble and the base!
Being the same in lacking knowledge,
their virtue did not depart;
being the same in lacking desire,
this is called pristine simplicity (sù pǔ);
in pristine simplicity, the people's nature is obtained.
But when the sage (shèng rén) arrived,
hobbling and bustling for benevolence (rén),
