tripping and stumbling for righteousness (yì),
then the world began to doubt;
indulging wantonly in music (yuè),
When simplicity is abandoned for ritual,
the world begins to divide.
Therefore, if pure simplicity is not destroyed,
who would make sacrificial vessels!
If white jade is not broken,
who would make guī (圭) and zhāng (璋) ritual objects!
If morality (dào dé) is not abandoned,
where would one get benevolence and righteousness (rén yì)!
If natural dispositions are not separated,
what use is there for ritual and music (lǐ yuè)!
If the five colors are not mixed,
who would make patterns!
If the five tones are not disordered,
who would match the six lǜ (律) pitch pipes!
Now, to destroy simplicity to make implements
is the craftsman's fault;
to destroy morality to create benevolence and righteousness
is the sage's mistake.
Now, horses, when living on land, eat grass and drink water,
when happy, they intertwine necks and rub against each other,
when angry, they separate backs and kick each other.
This is all horses know.
Now, adding a yoke and bridle,
aligning them with forehead ornaments,
then horses know to be wary
and how to resist, snatch, and deceive by
cunningly biting the bit and stealing the reins.
Therefore, the fact that horses become knowledgeable and can be led to theft is the fault of Bólè.
In the time of Xù Hūshì,
the people lived without knowing what to do,
traveled without knowing where to go,
sucking on food and playing,
patting their bellies and wandering about.
The people were capable of only this.
But when the sages arrived,
they bent and twisted ritual and music
to correct the form of the world,
and hung up tiptoeing benevolence and righteousness
to comfort the hearts of the world.
And then the people began to stand on tiptoe, becoming fond of knowledge,
competing to return to profit,
and could not be stopped.
This is also the fault of the sages.
Qiè Qiè, Chapter Ten.
If one prepares to guard against those who break open boxes, probe bags, and open chests to steal,
then one must tighten the cords,
and secure the locks and keys.
This is what the world calls wisdom.
However, when the great thief arrives,
he carries the chests on his back, lifts the boxes,
and carries the bags away, hurrying off,
only fearing that the cords and locks are not secure enough.
In that case, are those whom the village calls "wise"
not accumulating wealth for the great thief?
Therefore, let us try to discuss this:
of those whom the common people call "wise,"
are there any who are not accumulating wealth for the great thief?
Of those who are called "sages,"
are there any who are not guarding it for the great thief?
How do we know this to be true?
In the past, in the state of Qí, neighboring towns looked upon each other,
the sounds of chickens and dogs could be heard between them,
the places where nets were spread,
the places where plows and hoes pierced the earth,
extended over two thousand *lǐ*.
Within all four borders,
the means by which ancestral temples, altars to the gods of earth and grain,
and the administration of towns, dwellings, districts, neighborhoods, villages, and hamlets were established,
has it ever not been based on the laws of the sages?
Yet Tián Chéngzǐ killed the ruler of Qí in a single day and stole his state.
What he stole, was it only the state?
He also stole the sages' laws of wisdom along with it.
Therefore, Tián Chéngzǐ had the name of a thief,
yet lived in the security of Yáo and Shùn;
small states did not dare to criticize him,
large states did not dare to punish him,
and for twelve generations, he possessed the state of Qí.
Is this not stealing the state of Qí
and using the sages' laws of wisdom
to guard his thieving body?
Let me attempt to discuss it:
those whom the common people call supremely wise,
are there any who do not accumulate wealth for great thieves?
Those whom they call supremely sage,
are there any who do not guard possessions for great thieves?
How do we know this to be true?
In the past, Lóng Féng was executed,
Bǐ Gān was disemboweled,
Cháng Hóng was dismembered,
and Zǐ Xū was ground into paste;
thus, the virtue of these four men
did not save them from being killed.
Therefore, the followers of Zhí asked Zhí, saying:
"Does thievery also have a Way (道, *dào*)?"
Zhí said:
"Where is there that it does not have a Way!"
To make a reckless guess about the treasure in a house
is sagacity;
to enter first
is courage;
to exit last
is righteousness;
to know what is possible and what is not
is knowledge;
to divide equally
is benevolence.
There has never been anyone in the world who could become a great thief without possessing these five qualities.
From this, we can see that
If good people do not obtain the Dao of the sage,
they will not be established;
Zhí (盜跖) does not obtain the Dao of the sage,
he will not act.
If the good people in the world are few
and the bad people are many,
then the benefits of the sage to the world are few
and the harm to the world is much.
Therefore, it is said:
"If the lips are exhausted, the teeth will be cold;
if the wine of Lǔ (魯) is thin, then Hándān (邯鄲) will be besieged;
when a sage is born, great robbers arise."
Reject and strike down the sages,
release and abandon the thieves,
and the world will begin to be governed.
For when the rivers are exhausted, the valleys are empty;
when the hills are leveled, the depths are filled.
When the sage is already dead,
then the great robbers will not arise,
and the world will be peaceful and without incident.
If the sage does not die,
the great robbers will not cease.
Although one honors the sage to govern the world,
this is to greatly benefit the robber Zhí (盜跖).
If you make bushels and pecks to measure with them,
then [the robbers] will steal them along with the bushels and pecks;
if you make balances to weigh with them,
They are taken along with scales and measures and stolen;
If one makes tallies and seals to give credence to them,
they are taken along with the tallies and seals and stolen;
if one establishes benevolence and righteousness to rectify them,
they are taken along with benevolence and righteousness and stolen.
How do we know that this is so?
He who steals a hook is punished,
he who steals a state becomes a feudal lord.
At the gates of the feudal lords, benevolence and righteousness are preserved.
Is this not stealing benevolence, righteousness, sagacity, and knowledge?
Therefore, drive out the great robber,
expose the feudal lords,
stealing benevolence and righteousness,
along with the benefits of measures of capacity, weight, and the tallies and seals;
even with the reward of carriages and crowns
it cannot be encouraged,
and the power of axes and halberds
cannot prohibit it.
This is valuing the robber Zhí (盜跖) and making them impossible to prohibit;
this is the fault of the sages.
Therefore it is said:
"Fish should not be taken from the deep,
the sharp weapons of the state should not be shown to the people."
Those sages,
are the sharp weapons of the world,
not that by which to enlighten the world.
Therefore, abandon sagacity and discard knowledge,
Then the great thieves will cease;
discarding jade and destroying pearls,
petty thieves will not arise;
burning tallies and breaking seals,
then the people will be simple and unrefined;
smashing measures and breaking scales,
then the people will not contend;
exhausting and destroying the sacred laws of the world,
only then can the people begin to engage in discussion.
Disrupting the six musical modes,
melting down and destroying the *yú* reeds and *sè* zithers,
stopping the ears of blind musician Kuàng,
then the people of the world will begin to contain their own wisdom;
obliterating literature,
scattering the five colors,
gluing the eyes of Lí Zhū,
then the people of the world will begin to contain their own vision;
destroying and eliminating hooks and lines
and discarding compasses and squares, cutting off the fingers of artisan Chuí,
then the people of the world will begin to contain their own skill.
Therefore it is said:
"Great skill appears clumsy."
Erasing the conduct of Zēng and Shǐ,
silencing the mouths of Yáng and Mò,
casting aside benevolence and righteousness,
then the virtue of the world will begin to be mysteriously unified.
When people contain their own vision,
then the world will not be eroded;
When people contain their intelligence,
then the world will not be burdened.
When people contain their wisdom,
then the world will not be confused.
When people contain their virtue,
then the world will not be perverse.
Those like Zēng (曾), Shǐ (史), Yáng (楊), Mò (墨), Shī Kuàng (師曠), Gōng Chuí (工倕), and Lí Zhū (離朱),
all
externally established their virtue
and used it to agitate and disturb the world,
which the law cannot prevent.
Do you alone not know of the age of perfect virtue?

In the past, in the time of Róngchéng Shì (容成氏), Dàtíng Shì (大庭氏), Bóhuáng Shì (伯皇氏), Zhōngyāng Shì (中央氏), Lìlù Shì (栗陸氏), Líchù Shì (驪畜氏), Xuānyuán Shì (軒轅氏), Hèxū Shì (赫胥氏), Zūnlú Shì (尊盧氏), Zhùróng Shì (祝融氏), Fúxī Shì (伏戲氏), and Shénnóng Shì (神農氏),
the people used knotted cords for record-keeping,
found their food sweet,
found their clothing beautiful,
enjoyed their customs,
were content in their dwellings,
neighboring countries overlooked each other,
the sounds of chickens and dogs were heard between them,
and the people until old age and death
did not interact with each other.
In such a time as this,
perfect order was achieved.
Now it has come to the point of making the people crane their necks and stand on tiptoe, saying:
"So-and-so has a worthy person."
They bring food and rush to him,
Then inwardly they abandon their parents,
and outwardly they forsake serving their lords.
Their footprints connect to the borders of the various lords,
and their cart tracks extend beyond a thousand *lǐ*.
This is because the ruler excessively delights in knowledge.
If the ruler truly delights in knowledge but lacks the proper way,
then the world will be greatly disordered.
How do we know this is true?
If knowledge of bows, crossbows, nets, and traps is abundant,
then birds will be disordered above;
if knowledge of hooks, bait, nets, and traps is abundant,
then fish will be disordered in the water;
if knowledge of platforms, nets, and snares is abundant,
then beasts will be disordered in the marshes;
if knowledge of deceit, gradual poisoning, *xiéhuá* (tricky and slippery),
hardness/whiteness (堅白, *jiānbái*) arguments, dissection/dirt arguments,
and variations of sameness and difference is abundant,
then the common people will be confused by debates.
Therefore, the world is repeatedly greatly disordered,
and the fault lies in the love of knowledge.
Thus, everyone in the world knows to seek what they do not know,
but no one knows to seek what they already know;
everyone knows to criticize what they do not deem good,
but no one knows to criticize what they already deem good.
This is the reason for great disorder.
Thus, above, it contradicts the brightness of the sun and moon;
below, it diminishes the essence of mountains and rivers;
Causing the benefits of the four seasons to be disrupted;
the timid and weak insects,
and the creatures that fly and flutter,
none of them can maintain their proper nature.
How disastrously has the love of knowledge disordered the world!
Those from the Three Dynasties downwards are the examples of this.
Abandoning the diverse and natural people, they delight in flattering and subservient officials.
Rejecting the tranquil and effortless way, they delight in those who hum and chant meanings.
This constant humming and chanting has already thrown the world into chaos!
Chapter Eleven: Zài Yòu (Letting Be)
I have heard of letting the world be,
but I have not heard of governing the world.
Letting be [zài zhī] means
being afraid that the world will become dissolute in its nature;
yòu zhī (allowing) means
being afraid that the world will change its virtue.
If the world does not become dissolute in its nature,
and does not change its virtue,
then would there be anyone to govern the world?
In the past, when Yáo governed the world,
he made the world rejoice joyfully,
and people delighted in their nature.
This was not tranquility.
When Jié governed the world,
he made the world weary and exhausted,
and people suffered in their nature.
This was not pleasure.
Now, to be neither at ease nor happy
is not virtue.
That which is not virtue and can last for a long time, does not exist under Heaven.
When a person is greatly pleased,
it leans towards *yáng*;
when greatly angered,
it leans towards *yīn*.
When *yīn* and *yáng* both lean to one side,
the four seasons do not arrive,
the harmony of cold and heat cannot be achieved,
and it will in turn harm a person’s physical form!
It causes people’s joy and anger to lose their proper place,
their dwelling and abode to lack constancy,
their thoughts and considerations not to be self-obtained,
the middle way not to form a pattern.
Thereupon, the world begins with *qiáo jí zhuó zhì* [contorted and perverse dispositions],
and then there are the actions of Dào Zhí and Zēng Shǐ.
Therefore, to take all under Heaven to reward their goodness is not enough,
and to take all under Heaven to punish their evil is not sufficient.
Thus, the greatness of all under Heaven
is not enough for reward and punishment.
Those from the Three Dynasties onwards
are busily engaged
in using rewards and punishments as their business.
How can they have time to secure the essence of their nature and life!
Furthermore, to advocate brightness [intelligence]?
That is being excessive in form/color [beauty];
Are you advocating cleverness?
It is indulging in sound.
Are you advocating benevolence?
It is disrupting virtue.
Are you advocating righteousness?
It is violating principle.
Are you advocating ritual?
It is a matter of skill.
Are you advocating music?
It is a matter of indulgence.
Are you advocating sagacity?
It is a matter of art.
Are you advocating knowledge?
It is a matter of fault.
If the world is to find peace in its inherent nature and feelings,
these eight things, their existence is acceptable, their absence is acceptable.
If the world is not to find peace in its inherent nature and feelings,
these eight things
will then be carved, rolled up, bundled into bags,
and used to throw the world into chaos.
And the world then begins to revere and cherish them—
how deeply the world is deluded!
How can one simply pass by such faults and abandon them?
Instead, they purify themselves with fasting to speak of them,
kneel and sit upright to promote them,
beat drums and sing to dance for them.
What should I do with such things?
Therefore, when the *jūnzǐ* 君子 (gentleman, ruler) has no choice but to oversee the world,
Nothing is better than non-action (wú wéi).
Only through non-action
can one find peace in the true nature of one's life and destiny.
Therefore, valuing one's self more than governing the world,
one can be entrusted with the world;
cherishing one's self more than governing the world,
one can be relied upon to care for the world.
Therefore, if a noble person can but avoid disturbing their five internal organs,
and avoid exhausting their intelligence,
remaining like a corpse in stillness, yet appearing like a dragon,
being profoundly silent, yet sounding like thunder,
their spirit moving, and Heaven follows,
being leisurely in non-action,
and all things are "cooked" (brought to fruition) and accumulated.
What leisure would I have to govern the world!
Cuī Qú asked Lǎo Dān,
"If you do not govern the world,
how will you settle people’s hearts?"
Lǎo Dān said:
"You must be careful not to disturb people’s hearts.
The human heart rejects what is below
and advances toward what is above; being above and below is a kind of imprisonment and killing.
It is supple and gentle, yet stronger than the strong and rigid.
Being sharp, cutting, carving, and polishing,
its heat scorches like fire,
its coldness congeals like ice.
In the time it takes to bow one's head and look up again,
it can roam beyond the four seas twice.
In stillness, it resides deep and tranquil;
in action, it is suspended and heavenly.
That which overthrows pride and cannot be tied down,
is it not only the human heart!"
In the past, Huángdì 黄帝 first used benevolence and righteousness
to grasp the hearts of the people.
Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜 therefore wore their thighs bare and without down,
their shins without hair,
to nourish the bodies of all under Heaven,
worrying their five organs for the sake of benevolence and righteousness,
restraining their blood and qi to regulate laws and measures.
Yet even so, they still had no complete victory.
Yáo 堯 then exiled Huāndōu 讙兜 to Mount Chóng,
cast the Sānmiáo 三苗 into Sānwēi 三峗,
and banished Gònggōng 共工 to Yōudū 幽都.
This was not conquering all under Heaven.
When such measures extended to the Three Kings,
all under Heaven were greatly alarmed.
Below were Jié 桀 and Zhí 跖,
above were Zēng Zǐ 曾子 and Shǐ Shǐ,
and the Ru 儒 (Confucians) and Mò 墨 (Mohists) all arose together.
Thereupon, joy and anger suspected each other,
foolishness and wisdom deceived each other,
good and bad criticized each other,
falsehood and truth ridiculed each other,
and the world declined.
Great virtues differed,
and lives and destinies were confused and scattered.
The world values knowledge,
and the people are exhausted seeking it.
Consequently, chisels and saws are made,
plumb lines and ink markers bring death,
and mallets and chisels cause breaches.
The world is in great chaos and agitation,
the fault lies in agitating people's hearts.
Therefore, the wise hide themselves in the depths of great mountains, beneath cliffs and rocks,
while the rulers of ten thousand chariots
are filled with worry and trembling in their ancestral halls.
In the present age, those dying from punishment lie pillowed upon one another,
those wearing cangues jostle one another,
and those facing execution look upon one another in droves.
Yet the Ru (Confucians) and Mo (Mohists) then begin to stand on tiptoe and wave their arms within the confines of their restraints.
Alas, how extreme!
How extreme is their shamelessness and lack of self-awareness!
I do not know whether sagely knowledge is not the mortise for cangues and stocks,
or whether benevolence and righteousness are not the tenon for fetters and handcuffs.
How can one know that Zēng Shēn 曾參 and Shǐ Qiū 史䰯 are not the harbingers of Jié 桀 and Zhí 跖!
Therefore, it is said:
"Eliminate sageliness, discard knowledge, and the world will be greatly governed."
The Yellow Emperor Huángdì, having been established as the Son of Heaven for nineteen years,
and his commands were carried out throughout the land,
heard that Guǎngchéng Zǐ 廣成子 was on Mount Kōngtóng 空同,
so he went to see him,
and said:
"I have heard that you, master, are versed in the ultimate Dao,"
"I dare to ask about the essence of the ultimate Dao."
"I wish to take the essence of heaven and earth,"
"to aid the five grains and nourish the people."
"I also wish to govern Yin and Yang,"
"to fulfill the growth of all living beings."
"What should I do?"
Guǎngchéng Zǐ said:
"What you wish to ask about"
"is the substance of things;"
"what you wish to govern"
"is the remnants of things."
"Since you have governed the world,"
"the cloud vapors do not wait to gather before raining,"
"and the grasses and trees do not wait to turn yellow before falling."
"The light of the sun and moon has become increasingly dim."
"And the hearts of flatterers are sharp and cutting,"
"how could you possibly be worthy to speak of the ultimate Dao!"
Huángdì withdrew,
relinquished the world,
built a solitary chamber,
spread white reeds for a mat,
and lived in seclusion for three months.
He went again to invite him.
Guǎngchéng Zǐ lay with his head facing south.
Huángdì, going with the downward wind,
advanced on his knees,
bowed twice, kowtowed, and asked:
"I have heard that you, Master, are versed in the ultimate Dao.
May I venture to ask, how does one cultivate oneself to attain longevity?"
Guǎngchéngzǐ leapt up,
saying:
"Excellent question!
Come!
I will tell you about the ultimate Dao.
The essence of the ultimate Dao is profound and obscure;
the extremity of the ultimate Dao is dim and silent.
Do not look, do not listen,
embrace the spirit in tranquility,
and the form will naturally become upright.
Be certainly still, be certainly pure,
do not weary your form,
do not agitate your essence,
then you can attain longevity.
Let the eyes see nothing,
let the ears hear nothing,
let the mind know nothing,
and your spirit will guard your form,
and your form will then attain longevity.
Be careful with your inner self,
shut off your outer self,
much knowledge leads to ruin.
I will lead you to the realm above great brightness,
to the source of utmost Yang;
I will lead you into the gate of profound darkness,
to the source of utmost Yin.
Heaven and earth have their offices,
yin and yang have their storehouses.
Carefully guard your female form,
and things will naturally flourish.
I guarded its oneness to abide in its harmony,
therefore I have cultivated myself for twelve hundred years,
and my form has never aged."
Huángdì bowed again, kowtowing and saying,
"Guǎngchéngzǐ is what is meant by Heaven!"
Guǎngchéngzǐ said:
"Come!
I will tell you.
That thing is inexhaustible,
yet people all think it has an end;
that thing is immeasurable,
yet people all think it has a limit.
Those who attain my Dao, above are emperors and below are kings;
those who lose my Dao,
above see light
and below become earth.
Now, all things grow from the earth and return to the earth,
therefore I shall leave you,
enter the gate of the inexhaustible,
to roam in the field of the limitless.
I share light with the sun and moon,
I am constant with heaven and earth.
Approach me, and I am indistinct!
Keep me at a distance, and I am obscure!
"Are all the others going to die,
and I alone survive?!"
Yún Jiàng was traveling east,
passing the branches of the whirlwind (fú yáo zhī zhī),
and happened to encounter Hóng Méng.
Hóng Méng was just then patting his belly and hopping around for pleasure.
Yún Jiàng saw him,
was taken aback and stopped,
stood respectfully,
and said:
"Old Sir, who are you?
What are you doing here?"
Hóng Méng kept patting his belly and hopping around,
and replied to Yún Jiàng,
"Playing!"
Yún Jiàng said, "I wish to ask something."
Hóng Méng looked up at Yún Jiàng and said, "Alas!"
Yún Jiàng said, "The weather is not harmonious, the earth's energy is stagnant,
the six energies are not in balance, and the four seasons are not regulated.
Now I wish to combine the essence of the six energies
to nourish all living things.
What should be done about this?"
Hóng Méng patted his belly, hopped around, and shook his head, saying,
"I do not know!
I do not know!"
Yún Jiàng could not get an answer.
After another three years,
he traveled east,
Passing through the fields of the Sòng 宋 state,
I happened to meet Hóngméng 鴻蒙.
Yún Jiàng 雲將 was overjoyed,
hurried forward and said:
"Has Heaven forgotten me?
Has Heaven forgotten me?"
He bowed twice, kowtowed,
wishing to hear from Hóngméng 鴻蒙.
Hóngméng 鴻蒙 said:
"Floating aimlessly, not knowing what you seek;
Rushing madly, not knowing where you are going;
You bustle about restlessly, observing that which is without foundation.
How would I know anything!"
Yún Jiàng 雲將 said:
"I myself thought I was rushing madly,
and the people followed where I went;
I could not do otherwise than to lead the people,
but now the people are adrift. I wish to hear a word."
Hóngméng 鴻蒙 said:
"Disrupting the order of Heaven,
going against the nature of things,
dark Heaven cannot be completed;
scattering the herds of beasts,
and the birds all cry at night;
disaster reaches the grasses and trees,
misfortune reaches even the smallest insects.
Ah,
"It is governing people by excess!"
Yún Jiàng said, "In that case, what should I do?"
Hóng Méng said, "Alas,
how poisonous!
Gently, gently return."
Yún Jiàng said:
"I have encountered a heavenly difficulty;
I wish to hear a word."
Hóng Méng said:
"Alas!
Nourish your heart.
Simply dwell in non-action,
and things will transform themselves.
Cast off your form and body,
expel your cleverness,
forget the relationship with things;
greatly unite with the vast obscurity,
unbind your heart and release your spirit,
be blank and without a soul.
The myriad things in profusion,
each return to its root,
each return to its root
and are unaware;
muddled and chaotic,
never departing throughout life;
if they were to know it,
that would be to depart from it.
Do not ask its name,
Do not pry into its essence,
and things will naturally come into being on their own."
Yún Jiàng said:
"Heaven bestows virtue upon me,
and reveals silence to me.
By seeking it within myself,
I have now obtained it."
He bowed twice and kowtowed,
then rose, took his leave, and departed.
People in the world
all rejoice when others are like themselves
and resent others being different from themselves.
Wanting those who are like themselves
and disliking those who are different from themselves
stems from a desire to stand out from the crowd.
But those who desire to stand out from the crowd,
how can they ever truly stand out?
Relying on the crowd to secure
what one has heard is not as good as the skills of the multitude.
Yet, desiring to rule a state for others
is like grasping the benefits of the Three Kings
without seeing the harm they suffered.
This is to rule a state for others through mere luck.
How often can one be lucky enough to avoid losing the state of others?
The chances of preserving the state of others are less than one in ten thousand,
while the chances of losing the state of others are such that if one thing fails, ten thousand things are lost in excess.
Alas,
How ignorant are those who possess land!
To possess land
is to possess something great.
He who possesses something great
cannot be treated as a mere object.
When he treats things as things, yet is not treated as a thing,
then he is able to manipulate all things.
Understanding that one who manipulates all things is not a mere object,
how could he only be capable of governing the world and its people?
He goes in and out of the universe,
travels throughout the Nine Provinces,
goes alone and comes alone,
this is called being truly independent.
The person who is truly independent,
that is what is called supremely noble.
The teaching of a great person ([Dàrén]),
is like a shape casting its shadow,
a sound creating its echo.
When asked, he responds,
revealing all that he holds within,
and becomes a match for the world.
He dwells in the realm of no echo,
and travels in the realm of no direction.
Leading you to the endlessly swirling return,
to wander without end;
going in and out without boundaries,
and is without beginning along with the sun;
To praise and discuss the physical body
is to accord with Dà Tóng (大同),
to be in Dà Tóng (大同) and yet have no self.
Having no self,
how can one possibly possess anything!
Those who perceive possession
are the gentlemen of the past;
those who perceive non-possession
are friends of Heaven and Earth.
That which is humble yet cannot but be entrusted with,
is material things;
that which is lowly yet cannot but be relied upon,
is the people;
that which is concealed yet cannot but be done,
is affairs;
that which is coarse yet cannot but be displayed,
is law;
that which is distant yet cannot but be dwelt in,
is righteousness;
(Heaven)
but does not assist it;
(Virtue)
but not encumbered by it;
that which is intimate yet cannot but be broadened,
is benevolence;
that which is restrained yet cannot but be accumulated,
is ritual;
that which is central yet cannot but be elevated,
is virtue;
that which is unified yet cannot but be unchangeable,
is the Dao;
That which is divine and cannot but be done is
(Heaven).
(the Way)
but does not scheme;
(benevolence)
but does not rely on it;
(righteousness)
but does not accumulate it;
(ritual propriety)
but does not evade it;
he engages with affairs
but does not decline them;
(law)
but is not disordered by it;
he relies on the people
but does not belittle them;
he conforms to things
but does not abandon them.
Things are such that nothing can be enough to do them,
yet one cannot but do them.
(Heaven)
(Virtue);
(the Way)
has no means to be successful;
Those who are not clear about the Dao are
to be pitied!
What is the Dao?
There is the Dao of Heaven,
and there is the Dao of Humanity.
That which is honored through non-action is
the Dao of Heaven;
that which is burdened through action is
the Dao of Humanity.
The sovereign is the Dao of Heaven;
the minister is the Dao of Humanity.
The distance between the Dao of Heaven and the Dao of Humanity is vast;
it is imperative to examine them carefully.
*Tiāndì* Twelfth
Although Heaven and Earth are great,
their transformations are uniform.
Although the myriad things are numerous,
their governance is one.
Although the people are numerous,
their master is the ruler.
The ruler originates from virtue
and is completed by Heaven,
therefore it is said:
"The rulers of the ancient past governed the world through non-action,
relying solely on the virtue of Heaven."
Viewing words through the Dao, the rulers of the world are rectified;
Viewing distinctions through the lens of the Dao,
Viewing abilities through the lens of the Dao,
Viewing everything universally through the lens of the Dao,
the righteousness of ruler and subject becomes clear.
the offices of the world are well-governed.
the responses of all things are complete.
Therefore, that which penetrates Heaven and Earth
is Dé (virtue);
that which operates in all things
is the Dao;
that which governs people above
is shì (affairs);
that which can achieve something skillfully
is jì (skill).
Skill encompasses affairs,
affairs encompass righteousness,
righteousness encompasses virtue,
virtue encompasses the Dao,
and the Dao encompasses Heaven.
Therefore, it is said:
"The ancient keepers of the world
had no desires, and yet the world was satisfied;
they did nothing, and yet all things transformed;
they were profoundly still
and the people were settled."
The *Jì* (Record) says:
"Understanding the One,
all affairs are completed.
without having a heart that can be seized, even ghosts and spirits will submit."
Fūzǐ said:
"The Dao covers and supports Heaven and Earth and transforms and generates the myriad things.
How vast and great it is!
The junzi cannot but empty his heart for it.
To act through non-action is called Heaven.
To speak through non-speaking is called Virtue.
To love people and benefit things is called Ren.
To harmonize differences is called Greatness.
To act without being eccentric and strange is called Generosity.
To possess myriad differences is called Abundance.
Therefore, holding onto Virtue is called Discipline.
The completion of Virtue is called Establishment.
To follow the Dao is called Perfection.
Not allowing things to frustrate one's will is called Completion.
If the junzi is clear about these ten things,
then he will be concealing the greatness of his affairs within his heart,
and overflowing in his movements for the sake of the myriad things.
If one is like this,
he will hide gold in the mountains,
and hide pearls in the depths;
he will not covet wealth,
nor seek proximity to the noble and rich;
he will not rejoice in longevity,
nor grieve over early death;
he will not glory in success,
nor feel ashamed of poverty;
Not clinging to the profits of a single generation
to use as personal gain,
nor regarding the ruling of the world
as a position of obvious prominence.
When prominence is achieved, there is clarity;
all things are unified in one storehouse;
death and life share the same form."
Fūzǐ said:
"Indeed, the Dao
is profound in its dwelling place,
and vast in its purity.
Without metal and stone, there is no way to make sound.
Therefore, metal and stone have sounds,
but they do not resonate without being struck.
What thing is able to define all creation!
As for those of kingly virtue,
they remain simple and ashamed of being engrossed in affairs,
they establish the root and origin
and comprehend the divine.
Therefore, their virtue is broad,
and what emanates from their hearts is embraced by all things.
Thus, form cannot come into being without the Dao,
and life cannot be illuminated without virtue.
Preserving form exhausts life,
establishing virtue illuminates the Dao—
are these not the characteristics of those with kingly virtue?
How vast!
Suddenly emerging,
He stirs suddenly,
and all things follow him!
This is what is meant by a person of kingly virtue.
He sees in the dimness,
he hears in the silence.
In the dimness,
he alone perceives the dawn;
in the silence,
he alone hears harmony.
Therefore, profoundly deep and still more profound, he is able to understand things;
divinely spiritual and still more divinely spiritual, he is able to grasp the essence;
therefore, when he interacts with all things,
he reaches non-being and supplies their needs,
he directs them according to the times and meets their resting places,
great and small, long and short, near and far,
each has its provision."
The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) traveled north of the Red River (Chìshuǐ),
ascended the Hill of Kunlun (Kūnlún) and looked south,
then returned,
losing his dark pearl.
He sent Knowledge (Zhī) to seek it
but he could not find it,
he sent Clear Vision (Lízhū) to seek it
but he could not find it,
he sent Sharp Tongue (Chīgòu) to seek it
but he could not find it either.
Then he sent Image-Vague (Xiàngwǎng),
Xiàng Wǎng obtained it.
Huángdì said,
"How extraordinary!
Can Xiàng Wǎng actually obtain it?"
Yáo's teacher was Xǔ Yóu,
Xǔ Yóu's teacher was Niè Quē,
Niè Quē's teacher was Wáng Ní,
Wáng Ní's teacher was Bèi Yī.
Yáo asked Xǔ Yóu,
"Can Niè Quē be matched with Heaven?
I wish to employ Wáng Ní to persuade him."
Xǔ Yóu said,
"How dangerous! To treat the world like mere refuse!
Niè Quē, as a person, is clever and insightful,
quick and efficient in calculations,
and his nature surpasses others;
yet he relies on human (attributes) to receive Heaven.
He is meticulous about avoiding faults,
but does not know the source from which faults arise.
To match him with Heaven?
He will surely ride on human (attributes) and lack Heaven,
and he will certainly focus on himself and become different in form,
he will surely value knowledge and rush around like fire,
he will surely be made to serve ends,
he will surely be bound by things,
he will surely look around and things will respond,
he will surely cater to the suitability of the masses,
he will surely transform with things,
and has never had any constancy.
How can such a one be worthy to be matched with Heaven?
However,
having clans
and having ancestors,
one can be a father to many,
but cannot be a father to many fathers.
Order is the prelude to chaos,
facing north (as a subject) is the source of calamity,
facing south (as a ruler) is the origin of treachery."
Yáo observed the region of Huá.
The border guard of Huá said:
"Oh, Sage!
Please let me wish the sage well,
may the sage have long life."
Yáo said:
"Decline."
"May the sage be wealthy."
Yáo said:
"Decline."
"May the sage have many sons."
Yáo said:
"Decline."
The border guard said:
"Longevity, wealth, and many sons
are what people desire.
You alone do not desire them, why?"
Yáo said:
"Having many sons leads to many fears,
being wealthy leads to many affairs,
and living long leads to many humiliations.
These three are not the means to cultivate virtue,
therefore I decline."
The border official said:
"At first, I thought you were a sage,
but now you are merely a *jūnzǐ*.
Heaven gives birth to the myriad people,
and inevitably bestows upon them duties.
If you have many sons and give them duties,
then what fear is there to have!
If you are wealthy and let people share it,
then what affairs are there to have!
The sage,
lives like a quail and eats like a fledging,
moves like a bird without leaving a trace;
when the world is governed well,
then he flourishes along with all things;
when the world is not governed well,
then he cultivates his virtue and seeks seclusion;
growing weary of the world after a thousand years,
he departs and ascends as an immortal;
riding upon white clouds,
he arrives at the emperor's homeland;
the three calamities do not befall him,
and his body is always without misfortune;
then what humiliation is there to have!"
The border official left him.
Yáo followed him,
and said,
"May I ask?"
The border official said, "Withdraw already!"
Yáo governed the world,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo was established as a feudal lord.
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn, Shùn passed the throne to Yǔ,
and Bóchéng Zǐgāo
resigned from being a feudal lord and farmed.
Yǔ went to see him,
and found him farming in the fields.
Yǔ hurried to a position downwind,
stood and asked him, saying,
"In the past, when Yáo governed the world,
you, sir, were established as a feudal lord.
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed the throne to Yǔ,
and you, sir, resigned from being a feudal lord and farmed.
May I venture to ask what the reason for this is?"
Zǐgāo said,
"In the past, when Yáo governed the world,
the people were encouraged without rewards,
and the people were in awe without punishments.
Now you use rewards and punishments,
and the people are becoming unkind.
Virtue is declining from this point,
laws are being established from this point,
The chaos of later generations began from this.
Fūzǐ, are you about to leave?
"Do not neglect my work!"
He plowed leisurely, without looking back.
In the beginning of the Great Beginning, there was nothingness,
Nothingness had no name;
The origin of Oneness,
There was Oneness, but it had not yet taken form.
Things are able to be born,
This is called Dé (virtue);
That which has not yet taken form has divisions,
Moreover, it is naturally without gaps,
This is called Mìng (fate/destiny);
It remains and moves, thereby producing things,
Things are formed, and then life arises,
This is called Xíng (form);
Form protects the spirit,
Each has its own rules and regulations,
This is called Xìng (nature).
Cultivating the nature to return to Dé,
Dé reaches the point of being identical to the beginning.
Identical then becomes emptiness,
Emptiness then becomes greatness.
They join their beaks and sing;
Their beaks join and sing,
They are in harmony with Heaven and Earth.
Their harmony is continuous,
Acting as if foolish and muddled,
This is called profound virtue,
Being in accordance with the Great Conformity.
Fūzǐ (夫子) asked Lǎodān (老聃), saying:
"There are those who govern the Way as if they are abandoning it;
Is it permissible or not?
Is it so or not?
Debaters have a saying,
'Separating hardness and whiteness is like suspending a universe.'
If this is so, then can they be called sages?"
Lǎodān (老聃) said:
"These are all easy tricks, concerned with
Laboring the body and frightening the mind.
A dog held back becomes a burden;
The agility of monkeys and apes comes from the mountains and forests.
Qiū (丘), I will tell you,
What you cannot hear,
and what you cannot speak.
Those that have head and feet but no mind or ears are many;
Those that have form, and those that have no form or shape
and yet all exist, are completely nonexistent.
Its movement is stillness;
Its death is life;
Its decline is rise.
This is again not what it is because of.
There is governing that lies in people,
Forgetting things,
To forget about Heaven,
is called forgetting oneself.
A person who forgets oneself
is said to enter into Heaven."
Jiāng Lǘ Miǎn saw Jì Chè and said,
"The Lord of Lǔ said to Miǎn, 'Please accept my instruction.'
I declined but did not receive permission
and have already told him.
I don't know if it was appropriate,
please try to recommend it.
I said to the Lord of Lǔ,
'You must be reverent and frugal,
and select those who are publicly loyal
without favoritism.
What subject would dare not be harmonious?'"
Jì Chè laughed stiffly and said,
"Sir, your words regarding the virtue of an emperor
are like a praying mantis raising its arms to block a chariot wheel; it is certain to be unequal to the task.
Moreover, if it were like that,
then his own actions would be hasty, endangering
his viewing tower,
many things would go there,
and those seeking to leave their footprints would be many."
Jiāng Lǘ Miǎn looked around in surprise and said,
"Miǎn is confused by what you say.
However,
I would like the master to speak of its influence."
Jì Chè said,
"When a great sage governs the world,
he stirs and moves the hearts of the people,
causing them to embrace teachings and change their customs.
He utterly eliminates their thievish hearts
and leads them all to pursue their own singular aspirations,
as if it were their own nature guiding them.
And the people do not know the reason why it is so.
If it were so,
would it not be a case of elder brother Yáo 舜 and younger brother teaching the people,
in a state of vast and confused ignorance?
Desiring to be united in virtue, their hearts would dwell in peace."
Zǐ Gòng 子貢 was traveling south to Chǔ 楚,
and returning to Jìn 晉.
He passed through the south bank of the Hàn 漢 River,
and saw an old man who was about to make garden beds.
He was digging a tunnel to enter the well,
carrying a jug to draw water for irrigation.
He was straining himself and working very hard,
but the results were meager.
Zǐ Gòng 子貢 said, "There is a tool here that
can irrigate a hundred beds in a day,
requiring very little effort and yielding great results.
Would you not like to use it?"
The gardener looked up and asked,
"What is it like?"
He said,
"It is a device made of wood,
heavy at the back and light at the front,
Drawing water is like pulling [it up] [from a well],
the speed is like pouring hot soup;
its name is a shadoof."
The gardener angrily changed countenance and laughed, saying:
"I have heard from my teacher
that he who uses machines
is sure to have machine affairs;
he who has machine affairs
is sure to have a machine heart.
If the machine heart exists in the breast,
then pure simplicity is not complete;
if pure simplicity is not complete,
then the spirit's life is unsettled;
he whose spirit's life is unsettled
is not a vehicle for the Dao.
It's not that I don't know [about it],
but I am ashamed to do it."
Zǐgòng was taken aback and ashamed,
and lowered his head without answering.
After a while,
the gardener said:
"What sort of person are you?"
He said:
"A disciple of Kǒng Qiū."
The gardener said:
"Are you not one of those who is broadly learned to imitate a sage,
who acts grandly to overshadow the masses,
who sings sad songs on a single string to sell his reputation to the world?
You are about to forget your spirit and energy,
abandon your physical form,
and perhaps be close to achieving it!
If you cannot even govern your own person,
how can you have time to govern the world?
Go now,
do not neglect my affairs!"
Zǐ Gòng 子貢 was humbled and distraught,
anxious and ill at ease.
He walked thirty *lǐ* before recovering.
His disciples said:
"Who was that person just now?
Why did our master change his expression and lose color upon seeing him,
and remain uneasy all day long?"
He said: "At first, my master thought that everyone in the world was alike.
He didn't know there was another person like that.
I heard from my master that
affairs should be sought that are manageable,
achievements should be sought that are successful.
Using little effort
and seeing much accomplishment,
that is the way of the sage.
But now it is not so.
One who holds to the Dao has complete virtue,
one who has complete virtue has a complete form,
one who has a complete form has a complete spirit.
One who has a complete spirit
This is the Way of the Sage.
It rests on life, walking alongside the people,
yet without knowing where it is going.
How vast and purely complete it is!
Calculating profit and ingenious devices will inevitably cause one to forget the heart of that person.
As for that person,
they will not go where their will does not lead them,
they will not do what their heart does not prompt them to.
Even if the world praises them,
if they achieve what they seek,
they will loftily not look back.
Even if the world criticizes them,
if they lose what they seek,
they will nonchalantly not accept it.
The world's criticism or praise
neither benefits nor harms them.
This is what is called a person of complete virtue!
I speak of a people adrift like waves."
He returned to Lǔ (魯)
and told Kǒngzǐ (孔子).
Kǒngzǐ said:
"That person is borrowing the techniques of the primordial chaos!
He knows one thing,
but doesn't know the other;
he governs his inner self,
but does not govern his outer self.
To comprehend brightness and enter simplicity,
to act without action and return to the uncarved block,
One who embodies the essence of things and embraces the spirit,
in order to wander among the customs of the world,
would you be greatly surprised by this?
Moreover, the arts of Húndùn Shì,
how could you and I possibly understand them!"
Zhuōnmáng was about to go east to the Great Ravine,
when he happened to meet Yuànfēng on the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Yuànfēng said:
"Where are you going?"
He said:
"I am going to the Great Ravine."
He said:
"What for?"
He said:
"The Great Ravine, as a thing,
is filled without being full,
and drawn from without being exhausted;
I am going to wander there."
Yuànfēng said:
"Does the master have no concern for the cross-eyed people?
I wish to hear about sage governance."
Zhuōnmáng said:
"Sage governance?
Offices are bestowed without losing their appropriateness,
talents are selected and promoted without losing their abilities,
all matters are fully understood
and actions are carried out according to what is needed,
actions and words are spontaneous, and the world is transformed,
He scratches his head and points around,
and the people from all directions come without exception.
This is called sage governance."
"I wish to hear about the Person of Virtue."
He said:
"The Person of Virtue
dwells without thinking,
acts without deliberation,
and does not harbor right and wrong, beauty and ugliness.
Within the Four Seas, sharing benefit is called joy,
and sharing provisions is called peace.
He is as lost as an infant who has lost its mother,
and as bewildered as one who walks and loses their way.
His wealth and resources are abundant
but he does not know where they come from,
his food and drink are sufficient
but he does not know where it originates.
This is called the countenance of the Person of Virtue."
"I wish to hear about the Divine Person."
He said:
"The highest spirit rides the light,
and vanishes with the form.
This is called illuminating the vastness.
He commits his life and exhausts his emotions,
heaven and earth rejoice
and all affairs are extinguished,
all things return to their original state.
This is called undifferentiated darkness."
Mén Wúguǐ and Chì Zhāngmǎnjī observed the army of King Wǔ.
Chì Zhāngmǎnjī said:
"It cannot compare to the time of Yú the Great!
That is why we are free of this trouble."
Mén Wúguǐ said:
"Was the world equally well-governed
and then Yú the Great governed it?
Or was it governed after it was in chaos?"
Chì Zhāngmǎnjī said:
"To wish for the world to be equally well-governed,
why would one plan using the model of Yú the Great?
Yú the Great is like medicine for a sore;
like using a wig to cover baldness,
or seeking a doctor when sick.
A filial son administers medicine to heal his loving father,
but his face is filled with anxiety;
a sage would be ashamed of that.
In an age of supreme virtue,
they do not value the wise,
nor employ the capable;
those above are like signposts,
the people are like wild deer;
they are upright and do not know that it is righteousness,
they love each other and do not know that it is benevolence,
they are sincere and do not know that it is loyalty,
they act appropriately and do not know that it is trustworthiness,
they move about and employ each other,
without thinking it is a gift.
Shì gù xíng ér wú jì,
shì ér wú zhuàn." Therefore, they act without leaving a trace, and accomplish things without leaving behind any stories."
Xiào zǐ bù yú qí qīn,
zhōng chén bù chǎn qí jūn,
chénzǐ zhī shèng yě. "A filial son does not flatter his parents, and a loyal minister does not fawn upon his ruler; this is the height of being a subject and son."
Qīn zhī suǒ yán ér rán,
suǒ xíng ér shàn,
zé shìsú wèi zhī bùxiào zǐ;
jūn zhī suǒ yán ér rán,
suǒ xíng ér shàn,

zé shìsú wèi zhī bùxiào chén. "If one agrees with everything one's parents say and deems everything they do as good, then the common people will call him an unfilial son; if one agrees with everything one's ruler says and deems everything he does as good, then the common people will call him a disloyal minister."
Ér wèi zhī cǐ qí bìrán xié?
Shìsú zhī suǒwèi rán ér rán zhī,
suǒwèi shàn ér shàn zhī,

zé bù wèi zhī dào yú zhī rén yě. "But does one not know that this is necessarily the case? If one affirms what the common people call right and deems good what they call good, then one is not considered a person who flatters."
Ránzé sú gù yán yú qīn ér zūn yú jūn xié? "Then is it the case that common custom is stricter than parents and more esteemed than the ruler?"
Wèi jǐ dào rén,
zé bórán zuò sè;
wèi jǐ yú rén,
zé fúrán zuò sè. "If told that one is guiding others, one becomes indignant; if told that one is flattering others, one becomes indignant."
Ér zhōngshēn dào rén yě,
zhōngshēn yú rén yě,
hé pì shì cí
jù zhòng yě,
shì zhōngshǐ běnmò

bù xiāng zuò. "Yet one guides others one's entire life, flatters others one's entire life, uses metaphors and embellishes words, and gathers crowds; thus, the beginning and end, the root and the branch, do not align."
Chuí yīshāng,
shè cǎi sè,
To move one's countenance
to curry favor with the world,
yet not consider oneself to be uttering flattery,
joining the ranks of women;
to understand right and wrong,
yet not consider oneself to be among the masses—
this is the height of foolishness.
To know that one is foolish
is not great foolishness;
to know that one is deluded
is not great delusion.
The greatly deluded
remain unenlightened their entire lives;
the greatly foolish
remain unperceptive their entire lives.
If three people walk together and one is deluded,
the destination is still attainable,
because the deluded one is few.
If two are deluded,
then they will toil but not arrive,
because the deluded prevail.
But now, the world is deluded,
and even if I have aspirations,
they cannot be realized.
Is this not lamentable!
Loud sounds do not enter the ears of those in the neighborhood;
but to the tunes of "Zhé Yáng" 折楊 and "Huáng Huā" 皇荂,
they will burst into laughter.
Therefore, lofty words do not resonate in the hearts of the masses;
profound words are not uttered,
because vulgar words prevail.
Being confused by two clay pots,
one cannot achieve one's goal.
Now, being confused by the world,
even if I have aspirations,
how can they be realized?
To know that something is unattainable and yet force it is
yet another confusion.
Therefore, it is better to relinquish it
and not strive for it.
If one does not strive,
who can compare to one's freedom from worry?
A man from Lì
gives birth to his child in the middle of the night, and he hurriedly takes a torch to look at it,
anxiously fearing that it will resemble himself.
A hundred-year-old tree,
broken and made into a sacrificial vessel,
is adorned with blue and yellow colors,
but its stump lies in the ditch.
Comparing the sacrificial vessel to the stump in the ditch,
there is a difference in beauty and ugliness,
but their loss of original nature is the same.
Zhí and Zēng Shǐ, Zhí yǔ Zēng Shǐ, their actions and righteousness are different,
yet their loss of original nature is the same.
Furthermore, there are five ways to lose one's original nature:
First, the five colors confuse the eyes,
causing the eyes to be unclear.
Second, the five sounds confuse the ears,
causing the ears to be unhearing.
Third, the five odors assail the nose,
oppressing and bewildering the center of the forehead.
Fourth, the five flavors muddy the mouth,
causing the mouth to desire sharp tastes.
Fifth, pursuing and discarding things makes the heart slippery,
causing the nature to be flighty.
These five things
are all harmful to life.
Yet Yáng Mò 楊墨 begin to stray
and think themselves to have attained something;
this is not what I call attainment.
If being trapped is attainment,
can this be called attainment?
Then the dove and owl in a cage
can also be considered to have attained something.
Moreover, pursuing and discarding sounds and sights
is like piling firewood within oneself;
wearing a leather cap and kingfisher feather crown, holding a tablet, and wearing long sashes
is like restraining oneself externally.
Internally, one's limbs are stuffed full like a firewood fence,
externally, one is heavily bound by ropes.
Looking pleased with oneself while being trapped in the ropes
and thinking oneself to have attained something
is like a criminal with bound arms being counted off,
Even tigers and leopards in cages
can be considered captured.
*Tiāndào* Chapter Thirteen
The *Tiāndào* (Way of Heaven) operates without accumulation,
therefore all things are completed;
the *Dìdào* (Way of the Emperor) operates without accumulation,
therefore the world submits;
the *Shèngdào* (Way of the Sage) operates without accumulation,
therefore everything within the seas obeys.
Being enlightened about *Tiān* (Heaven),
understanding the *Shèng* (Sage),
and being adept in the six directions and opening the four directions through the virtues of the emperor and king,
in their self-cultivation,
they are profoundly and invariably in stillness.
The stillness of the sage
is not because they say stillness is good,
therefore they are still;
but because nothing among all things is sufficient to disturb their minds,
therefore they are still.
When water is still, it clearly reflects beard and eyebrows,
and is a level standard.
The master craftsman takes it as a model.
Water in stillness is still clear;
how much more so the spirit!
Is the heart of the sage still!
It is the mirror of Heaven and Earth,
the mirror of all things.
Now, emptiness, stillness, tranquility, indifference, silence, and inaction are
the equilibrium of Heaven and Earth
and the perfection of morality.
Therefore, emperors, kings, and sages find repose in them.
To repose is to be empty;
to be empty is to be full;
to be full is to be ordered.
To be empty is to be still;
to be still is to be active;
to be active is to attain.
To be still is to be inactive;
to be inactive is to hold responsible those who perform duties.
To be inactive is to be carefree;
to be carefree means that worries and troubles cannot abide,
and one's years are lengthened.

If the Dao could be given to others,
then everyone would give it to their children and grandchildren.
Yet it is impossible, for no other reason
than that there is no master within, and it does not stop;
externally, there is no equal, and it does not proceed.
That which comes from within,
not receiving from the outside,
the sage does not go out.
That which enters from the outside,
without a master within,
the sage does not conceal himself.
Fame is a public vessel;
it cannot be taken in excess.
Benevolence and righteousness are the temporary shelters of the former kings;
one can only stay for one night,
but cannot dwell there long.
To encounter them and make many demands is [unwise].
"The ultimate men of old
borrowed the Dao through benevolence,
lodged in righteousness,
in order to roam in the emptiness of freedom,
to eat from the fields of simplicity,
and stand in the gardens of non-borrowing.
Freedom is non-action;
simplicity is easy to nourish;
If you do not lend, do not go out.
The ancients called this a journey to seek truth.
Those who consider wealth as truth,
cannot relinquish emoluments;
those who consider fame as truth,
cannot relinquish reputation;
those who cherish power,
cannot share authority with others.
Grasping it, they tremble;
relinquishing it, they grieve;
and being utterly without discernment,
in order to spy on that which will not cease,
these are the people punished by Heaven.
Resentment, gratitude, taking, giving, remonstrance, instruction, life, death,
these eight,
are instruments of rectification;
only those who follow the great changes without being submerged are able to use them.
Therefore, it is said:
"Rectification is to be correct."
If in their hearts they think otherwise,
then the gate of Heaven will not open to them."
Kǒngzǐ saw Lǎodān
and spoke of benevolence and righteousness.
Lǎodān said:
"If you scatter chaff in the eyes,
then Heaven, Earth, and the four directions will change places;
if mosquitoes bite the skin,
then you will be kept awake all night.
Now, benevolence and righteousness,
when flaunted, will truly agitate our hearts;
no disorder is greater than this.
If you, my master, would have the world not lose its simplicity,
then you, my master, should also follow the wind and move,
consolidate virtue and establish yourself.
Why then so conspicuously
proclaim benevolence and righteousness, like someone carrying a large drum in search of a lost child?
The swan does not bathe daily to become white,
nor does the crow blacken itself daily to become black.
The naturalness of black and white
is not something requiring debate;
the appearance of reputation
is not something to be broadened.
When a spring dries up,
fish gather together on land,
moistening each other with their mouths,
wetting each other with their foam.
Better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes!"
Kǒngzǐ saw Lǎo Dān and returned,
and for three days did not speak.
His disciples asked,
"Master saw Lǎo Dān,
what lesson did you intend to learn?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Only now have I seen a dragon!
A dragon, combining to form a body,
scattering to form patterns,
He rides on the clouds and
nourishes himself with *yīn* and *yáng*.
My mouth is open
and I cannot close it;
my tongue is raised and I cannot speak clearly. What can I possibly advise Lǎo Dān?"
Zǐ Gòng said,
"So there are indeed people who dwell like corpses but appear like dragons,
who sound like thunder but are silent as a deep pool,
whose actions are like Heaven and Earth?
Could Cì also be allowed to see this?"
Thereupon, he used Kǒngzǐ's reputation to be introduced to Lǎo Dān.
Lǎo Dān was just sitting haughtily in the hall, preparing to respond,
and said faintly,
"My years are moving on,
what will you use to admonish me?"
Zǐ Gòng said,
"The Three Kings and Five Emperors governed the world differently,
but their aim to establish a reputation is the same.
Yet you alone think they are not sages,
why is that?"
Lǎo Dān said,
"Young man, come closer!
How do you say they are different?"
He replied,
"Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
Yǔ used labor,
and Tāng used arms.
Wén Wáng submitted to Zhòu
and dared not oppose him;
Wǔ Wáng opposed Zhòu
and was unwilling to submit.
Therefore, it is said that they were different."
Lǎo Dān said,
"Young man, come closer!
I will tell you about the governance of the world by the Three Kings and Five Emperors.
When the Huáng Dì governed the world,
he unified the minds of the people,
and when people's relatives died, they did not weep,
and the people did not criticize it.
When Yáo governed the world,
he made the people's hearts intimate,
and when people killed those who killed their relatives,
the people did not criticize it.
When Shùn governed the world,
he caused the people's hearts to contend,
and when pregnant women gave birth to children in ten months,
and the children could speak after five months,
and it was not until they were infants that they began to know who to rely on,
then people began to die young.
When Yǔ governed the world,
he caused the people's hearts to change,
and people had intentions, and soldiers had obedience.
Killing thieves was not considered killing people,
but only cultivating their own kind for the world,
and thus the world was greatly alarmed,
Both the Ru (Confucian) and Mo (Mohist) schools have arisen.
Their beginnings had principles,
but now they are like women. What is there to say?
Let me tell you,
the way the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors governed the world,
though called governing,
was the most chaotic possible.
The knowledge of the Three Sovereigns
was such that it contradicted the brightness of the sun and moon above,
and diverged from the essence of the mountains and rivers below,
and ruined the benefits of the four seasons in between.
Their knowledge was more cruel than the sting of a scorpion's tail.
Few beasts
could secure the true nature of their lives.
Yet they still considered themselves sages.
Are they not shameless?
How shameless they are!"
Zǐ Gòng stood fidgeting, ill at ease.
Kǒngzǐ said to Lǎo Dān:
"I, Qiū, have studied the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry), *Shū* (Classic of Documents), *Lǐ* (Classic of Rites), *Yuè* (Classic of Music),
*Yì* (Classic of Changes), and *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals)—the Six Classics.
I believed I had been at it for a long time
and understood their meaning.
I lobbied seventy-two rulers with bad intentions,
discussed the Dao of the former kings,
and clarified the deeds of Duke of Zhōu and Shào,
but not a single ruler found any of it useful.
How difficult it is! To persuade people is difficult,
to make the Dao clear is difficult indeed!"
Lǎozǐ said:
"Fortunate are you that you did not encounter a ruler of a well-governed age!
The "Six Classics"
are the traces left by the former kings,
how can they be the means by which they left traces!
What you are speaking of now
is also like traces.
Traces
are where the shoes have passed,
but are traces shoes?
White egrets gazing at each other, their pupils not moving,
are transformed by the wind;
insects,
the male chirping upwind,
the female responding downwind,
are transformed;
their kind naturally divides into male and female,
therefore they are transformed by the wind.
Nature cannot be changed,
destiny cannot be altered,
time cannot be stopped,
the Dao cannot be blocked.
If one attains the Dao,
there is nothing that cannot be done;
those who lose it,
find nothing that can be done."
Kǒngzǐ did not go out for three months,
and then returned to see him, saying:
"Qiū has grasped it.
Crows and magpies nurse their young,
fish breathe by blowing bubbles,
the slender wasp transforms,
when there is a younger brother,
the older brother cries.
For so long, I, Qiū, have not been transforming along with people!
If I do not transform along with people,
how can I transform others!"
Lǎozǐ said:
"Acceptable.
Qiū has grasped it!"
*Kè Yì* (Deliberate Effort), Fifteenth
To deliberately emphasize action,
to distance oneself from the world and differ from customs,
to make lofty pronouncements and voice grievances and criticisms,
is simply to strive for superiority;
these are the pursuits favored by those who dwell in mountains and valleys,
people not of the world,
those who wither and throw themselves into the abyss.
To speak of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and trustworthiness,
to practice reverence, frugality, deference, and yielding,
is simply to cultivate oneself;
these are the pursuits favored by those who live in times of peace,
people who teach and instruct,
Travel and dwelling are what scholars love.
Speaking of great achievements,
establishing great names,
regulating the rituals between ruler and subject,
rectifying superiors and inferiors,
is simply to govern well;
this is what court officials,
those who honor the ruler and strengthen the state,
and those who achieve merit and annex territories love.
Approaching thickets and marshes,
residing in secluded wilderness,
fishing in leisure,
doing nothing;
this is what gentlemen of the rivers and seas,
reclusive people,
and those who seek leisure love.
Blowing and breathing,
exhaling the old and inhaling the new,
moving like a bear and stretching like a bird,
is simply to prolong life;
this is what practitioners of *dǎoyǐn*,
those who nourish their bodies,
and those who seek the longevity of Péng Zǔ love.
As for those who are lofty without deliberate effort,
who cultivate themselves without benevolence or righteousness,
who govern well without功名 gōngmíng (merit and fame),
who are at leisure without rivers and seas,
who prolong life without *dǎoyǐn*,
There is nothing he does not forget,
there is nothing he does not possess,
calmly reaching the ultimate
and all beauties follow him.
This is the Dao of Heaven and Earth,
the virtue of the sage.
Therefore it is said:
Now, tranquility, serenity, stillness, silence, emptiness, and non-action,
these are the equilibrium of Heaven and Earth
and the essence of morality.
Therefore it is said:
The sage rests in them;
resting in them, he is calm and easy;
being calm and easy, he is tranquil and serene.
Being calm, easy, tranquil, and serene,
worries and anxieties cannot enter,
evil influences cannot attack;
therefore his virtue is complete and his spirit is not diminished.
Therefore it is said:
The sage's life is like the movement of Heaven;
his death is like the transformation of things;
in stillness, he shares virtue with the Yin;
in movement, he shares waves with the Yang;
he does not initiate blessings,
he does not begin calamities;
he responds only after being affected,
he moves only after being compelled,
He rises only when there is no other choice.
He discards knowledge and preconceived notions,
and follows the principles of Heaven.
Therefore, there are no natural disasters,
no encumbrances from things,
no human recriminations,
and no blame from ghosts.
His life is like floating,
and his death is like resting.
He does not ponder,
nor does he plan in advance.
He is radiant but not dazzling,
trustworthy but not expecting.
His sleep is without dreams,
and his waking is without worry.
His spirit is pure and unmixed,
and his soul is not weary.
Empty, still, quiet, and bland,
he thus aligns with the virtue of Heaven.
Therefore, it is said:
Grief and joy
are deviations of virtue;
happiness and anger
are excesses of the Way;
likes and dislikes
are losses of virtue.
Therefore, a heart without sorrow or joy
The ultimate in virtue;
is being unified and unchanging,
the ultimate in stillness;
is having nothing to oppose,
the ultimate in emptiness;
is not interacting with things,
the ultimate in simplicity;
is having nothing to resist,
the ultimate in purity.
Therefore it is said:
If the body is toiled without rest, it will become exhausted;
if the essence is used without ceasing, it will become weary;
if weary, then it will be depleted.
The nature of water
is that if not mixed, then it is clear;
if not stirred, then it is level;
If it is trapped and does not flow,
then it also cannot be clear.
This is an image of the virtue of Heaven.
Therefore it is said:
Pure and unmixed,
still, unified, and unchanging,
simple and without action,
moving and acting in accordance with Heaven,
this is the way to nourish the spirit.
Now, those who possess the swords of Gānyuè,
keep them in sheaths and store them away,
I dare not use it;
it is the ultimate treasure.
Its spirit reaches everywhere and flows together,
reaching everywhere without exception,
above it reaches to the heavens,
below it coils upon the earth,
transforming and nurturing all things,
it cannot be represented by an image;
its name is called Tóng Dì (同帝).
The way of pure simplicity,
only the spirit guards it;
guard it and do not lose it,
become one with the spirit;
the essence of oneness permeates everything,
uniting with the order of Heaven.
There is a saying amongst the common folk:
"The masses value profit,
upright men value reputation,
worthy men value aspiration,
and sages value essence."
Therefore, "simplicity" means
that it is unmixed with anything else;
"purity" means
that its spirit is not diminished.
One who can embody purity and simplicity
is called a true person (zhēn rén 真人).
Chapter Sixteen: Cultivating the Nature
Cultivating the nature within the common customs,
common learning seeks to restore its original state.
Slipping into desires within the common customs, thinking
to seek to attain clarity;
these are called obscured and ignorant people.
Those who governed in ancient times
nourished wisdom with tranquility.
Being born without using wisdom for action,
this is called using wisdom to nourish tranquility.
Wisdom and tranquility mutually nourish each other,
and harmony and reason arise from their nature.
Now, virtue is harmony;
the Way is reason.
Virtue encompasses everything,
this is benevolence;
the Way governs everything,
this is righteousness;
when righteousness is clear, things are intimate,
this is loyalty;
when the center is pure and substantial, and reverts to emotions,
this is joy;
when trustworthiness is practiced, demeanor and form conform to the rules,
this is ritual.
When ritual and music are universally practiced,
then the world will be in chaos.
They correct themselves and obscure their virtue;
if there is virtue, it does not overshadow;
If one covers (something), then it will inevitably lose its nature.
The people of old,
in the midst of chaos,
were able to obtain tranquility and detachment together with their generation.
At that time,
the *yīn* and *yáng* were harmonious and still,
ghosts and spirits did not disturb,
the four seasons followed their proper order,
the myriad things were not harmed,
the multitude of living beings did not die prematurely,
although people had knowledge,
they had no use for it.
This is called the ultimate unity.
At that time,
without anyone doing anything, things were always naturally so.
When virtue declined,
and it came to the time when Suìrén 燧人 and Fúxī 伏羲 first ruled the world,
therefore, there was accordance but not unity.
When virtue declined further,
and it came to the time when Shénnóng 神農 and Huángdì 黃帝 first ruled the world,
therefore, there was stability but not accordance.
When virtue declined further,
and it came to the time when Táng 唐 and Yú 虞 first ruled the world,
the currents of governance and transformation arose,
the original purity was fragmented and simplicity was scattered,
they departed from the Dao in order to do good,
they considered virtue to be dangerous and acted (accordingly),
Then they abandon their nature and follow their hearts.
The heart and its knowledge
are not enough to settle the world.
Then they embellish it with writing,
and augment it with vast learning.
Writing obscures substance,
and vast learning drowns the heart.
Then the people begin to be confused and disordered,
and there is no way to return to their original nature and feelings.
From this perspective,
the world has lost the Way (道, Dào),
and the Way has lost the world.
The world and the Way have lost each other.
How can a person of the Way flourish in the world?
And how can the world flourish in the Way?
The Way has no means to flourish in the world,
and the world has no means to flourish in the Way.
Even if a sage is not in the mountains and forests,
his virtue is hidden.
Because it is hidden,
he does not hide himself.
The so-called recluses of ancient times
did not conceal their bodies
so as not to be seen,
nor did they shut their mouths
so as not to speak,
nor did they hide their knowledge
yet does not flourish.
It is a great error in timing and fate.
If, when the time and fate are right, one greatly prevails throughout the world,
then in the end, one leaves no trace.
If, when the time and fate are not right,
one is greatly impoverished throughout the world,
then one deeply roots oneself in tranquility and waits.
This is the way to preserve oneself.
Those who preserved themselves in ancient times
did not use clever arguments to adorn their knowledge,
did not use knowledge to exhaust the world,
did not use knowledge to exhaust virtue,
but calmly remained where they were
and returned to their nature. What else would they do?
Why would *they* be like that?
The Way inherently cannot be implemented on a small scale,
and virtue inherently cannot be known by petty knowledge.
Petty knowledge harms virtue,
and petty actions harm the Way.
Therefore, it is said:
"Rectify oneself, and that is all."
Finding joy in completeness is called attaining one's aspirations.
What was called "attaining one's aspirations" in ancient times
did not refer to carriages and official hats,
but meant that there was nothing that could add to their joy.
What is called "attaining one's aspirations" nowadays
This refers to carriages and ceremonial caps.
Having carriages and ceremonial caps
is not intrinsic to one's nature or life;
they are merely things that happen to come, a temporary lodging.
Being a temporary lodging,
their arrival cannot be prevented,
nor can their departure be stopped.
Therefore, one does not indulge one's desires for carriages and ceremonial caps,
nor does one conform to vulgarity because of poverty and deprivation.
The joy of those is the same as the joy of these,
therefore there is no worry, and that's all.
Now, if one is not happy when the temporary lodging departs,
viewing it from this perspective,
even if there is joy,
it has never not been wasteful.
Therefore, it is said:
"Losing oneself in things
and losing one's nature in customs
is called a people who live in reversed order."
Autumn Floods, Chapter Seventeen
The autumn floods arrived on time,
and a hundred rivers poured into the Hé River.
The vastness of the Jīng River's flow,
between the banks and shores,
made it impossible to distinguish oxen from horses.
Thereupon, the Hé Bó (River Earl) was pleased and congratulated himself,
thinking that all the beauty in the world was contained within himself.
Floating downstream and traveling east,
I arrived at the North Sea.
Looking east,
I could not see the end of the water.
Thereupon, the Hé Bó began to change his expression,
gazing out at Rùo and sighing, saying:
"There is a saying among the rustic people that goes:
'Having heard a hundred principles,
one thinks no one is like oneself.'
This is what I am like.
Furthermore, I once heard of those who belittled Zhòng Ní's knowledge
and scorned Bó Yí's righteousness.
At first, I did not believe it;
now, seeing your inexhaustibility,
if I had not come to your door,
I would have been in danger,
and would have long been laughed at by those of great principles."
The Ruò of the North Sea said:
"A frog in a well cannot be talked to about the sea,
for it is limited by its confined space.
A summer insect cannot be talked to about ice,
for it is bound by the season.
A provincial scholar cannot be talked to about the Way,
for he is restricted by his teachings.
Now you have come out from the riverbank,
and gazed upon the great sea,
and then known your own insignificance.
You will now be able to be talked to about great principles.
Of all the waters under Heaven,
none is greater than the sea.
Ten thousand streams flow into it,
yet it is not known when they will stop without causing it to overflow;
the Wěilǘ drains it,
yet it is not known when it will cease without causing it to become empty;
spring and autumn do not change it,
and floods and droughts do not affect it.
This is because it surpasses the flow of the Jiāng and Hé rivers,
and cannot be measured.
Yet I have never been proud of this,
but rather compared my form to Heaven and Earth
and received my breath from Yin and Yang.
I am in the midst of Heaven and Earth
like a small stone or a small tree on a large mountain.
I consider myself to be small,
so why should I be proud of myself!
Consider the four seas within Heaven and Earth,
are they not like hollows in a great marsh?
Consider China within the seas,
is it not like a grain of rice in a vast granary?
The number of things
is called ten thousand,
and man is but one of them;
man occupies the nine provinces,
where grains are grown,
and boats and carts travel,
and man is but one of them.
Is this comparison to the myriad things not
like a hair on a horse's body?
What the Five Emperors linked together,
what the Three Kings contended for,
what the humane men worried about,
what the men of responsibility toiled over,
is all this.
Bó Yí declined it for the sake of reputation,
Zhòng Ní spoke of it as broad knowledge;
this is their self-aggrandizement,
isn't it like your previous self-aggrandizement regarding the water?"
The River God said,
"Then am I to consider myself great in relation to Heaven and Earth
and small in relation to a hair?
Is that acceptable?"
Spirit of the Northern Sea said, "No.
Measuring things, there is no limit;
time has no end;
divisions have no constancy;
beginning and end have no fixed cause.
Therefore, great knowledge observes the distant and the near;
thus, being small, it is not considered little;
being large, it is not considered much;
it knows that measurement is without limit.
Examining the past and present,
thus, being distant, it is not vexed;
picking things up, it does not stand on tiptoe;
it knows that time has no end.
Observing fullness and emptiness,
therefore, gaining does not bring joy,
and losing does not bring sorrow,
knowing that fortune has no constancy;
understanding the level path,
therefore, being born is not a delight,
and dying is not a calamity,
knowing that the end and the beginning cannot be fixed.
To calculate what people know
is not as good as what they do not know;
the time of their birth
is not as good as the time before they were born;
using their extremely small [knowledge] to seek to exhaust the realm of the extremely large,
therefore, they are confused and cannot find themselves.
Viewing it from this perspective,
how can one know that a hair's breadth is enough to determine the beginnings of the extremely small!
And how can one know that heaven and earth are enough to exhaust the realm of the extremely large!"
Hé Bó 河伯 said:
"Those who discuss the world all say:
'The most refined has no form,
the greatest cannot be encompassed.'
Is this truly the nature of things?"
Běi Hǎiruò 北海若 said:
"He who observes the large from the small does not see it completely,
and he who observes the small from the large does not see it clearly.
Now, refinement is the subtlety of the small;
a mound is the abundance of the large;
therefore, they differ in their suitability.
This is the nature of *shì* (勢, power, influence).
Now, that which is refined and that which is coarse,
both pertain to that which possesses form.
That which is without form
cannot be divided by numbers.
That which cannot be surrounded
cannot be exhausted by numbers.
That which can be spoken of in words is the coarse aspect of things;
that which can be reached through thought is the refined aspect of things.
That which cannot be discussed in words,
and that which the mind cannot perceive and attain,
is not limited to the refined or coarse.
Therefore, the actions of a great person (*dàrén*)
do not deviate into harming others,
nor are they overly concerned with benevolence and kindness.
Their actions are not for personal gain,
nor do they despise servants and subordinates.
They do not contend for goods and wealth,
nor are they overly concerned with yielding and deference.
They do not rely on others in their endeavors,
nor are they overly concerned with earning their own keep,
nor do they despise greed and corruption.
Their conduct differs from that of common people,
but they are not overly concerned with being different.
Their actions are based on following the crowd,
but they do not despise flattery and sycophancy.
The world's honors and emoluments are not enough to entice them,
nor are execution and shame enough to disgrace them.
Knowing that right and wrong cannot be distinguished,
and that the fine and the large cannot be measured.
It is said:
“The man of the Dao does not hear,
the possessor of supreme virtue does not attain,
the great man has no self."
This is the ultimate in reducing distinctions.”
The Hé Bó (河伯), the God of the Yellow River, said:
