The hammerer of hooks in Dàmǎ
was eighty years old
and did not miss a hair's breadth.
Dàmǎ said,
"Are you skillful?
Or do you have the Dao?"
He replied,
"Your servant has something he guards.
Your servant, at the age of twenty, was fond of playing the hammer-and-hook game.
I paid no attention to other things.
If it wasn't the hook, I wouldn't look at it.
Those who use it
borrow from those who don't use it, to further their own use,
how much more so for those who can't do without it!
Which thing doesn't rely on it!"
Rǎn Qiú asked Zhòng Ní,
"Can we know about the time before there was heaven and earth?"
Zhòng Ní said,
"We can.
The past is like the present."
Rǎn Qiú withdrew, having failed in his question.
The next day, he came to see him again,
and said,
"Yesterday, I asked
'Can we know about the time before there was heaven and earth?'
Master said,
'We can.
The past is like the present.'
Yesterday I understood clearly,
today I am confused.
May I ask what you mean?"
Zhòng Ní said,
"The clarity you had yesterday
was because a spiritual person first received it.
The confusion you have today
is because you are seeking it for someone who is not spiritual?
Without antiquity, without present,
without beginning, without end.
"Before having descendants, there are descendants,
is that permissible?"
Rǎn Qiú 冉求 did not answer.
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"Enough,
you cannot answer!
Do not use life to perpetuate life,
do not use death to resurrect life.
Is life and death something that requires waiting?
All things are unified in one body.
Is there something that exists before heaven and earth?
That which causes things to exist is not a thing itself.
The emergence of things cannot precede things,
yet it is as if there is something.
It is as if there is something,
endlessly.
The sage's love for people is also endlessly unceasing,
and is derived from this principle."
Yán Yuān 顏淵 asked Zhòng Ní 仲尼, saying:
"I have heard you say,
'Do not send forth,
do not receive.'
May I ask about its wanderings?"
Zhòng Ní 仲尼 said:
"The people of antiquity
outwardly transform, but inwardly do not transform;
People today,
are transformed internally but not externally.
Those who transform with things
are those who do not transform in one aspect.
What is it to transform and what is it not to transform?
How can they be in agreement and blend together?
Surely, they will not be compatible.
The parks of Xī Wéi Shì,
the gardens of Huángdì,
the palaces of Yǒu Yú Shì,
the chambers of Tāng and Wǔ.
People of virtue,
and those who are masters of the Rú (Confucian) and Mò (Mohist) schools,
therefore contend with each other with right and wrong,
let alone the people of today!
A sage dwells among things without harming them.
One who does not harm things,
cannot be harmed by things either.
Only those who suffer no harm,
are able to greet and meet people.
O mountains and forests!
O highlands and plains!
You make me joyfully happy!
Before the joy is finished,
sorrow then follows.
The coming of sorrow and joy, I cannot resist,
their departure I cannot stop.
Alas,
Worldly people are merely travelers in the realm of things!
They understand what they encounter
but do not understand what they do not encounter;
they understand what they can do
but do not understand what they cannot do.
To be without knowledge and without ability
is, in fact, what people cannot avoid.
To strive to avoid what people cannot avoid,
is that not also a tragedy?
The ultimate words abandon words;
the ultimate actions abandon actions.
To equalize what knowledge knows
is shallow indeed."
Gēngsāng Chǔ, Section Twenty-Three
Among the servants of Lǎo Dān was one named Gēngsāng Chǔ,
who partially attained Lǎo Dān's Dao.
He went north to live on Mount Wèilěi.
Those of his ministers who were markedly clever left him,
and those of his concubines who were conspicuously benevolent distanced themselves from him.
Those who were clumsy and ungainly lived with him;
those who were burdened with tasks served him.
After three years of residence,
Wèilěi became very fertile.
The people of Wèilěi spoke with each other, saying:
"When Master Gēngsāng first came,
we felt cleansed and different.
Now, if we calculate day by day, it is not enough;
He calculates his age and finds it more than sufficient.
Is he perhaps approaching sagehood!
Why don't you all together set him up as a *shī* [personator of the dead]
and offer prayers to him,
establish a local altar to him and worship him as the god of grain?"
Gēng Sāngzǐ 庚桑子 heard this
and faced south, but did not appear pleased.
His disciples found this strange.
Gēng Sāngzǐ 庚桑子 said:
"How are you disciples different from me?
When the spring *qì* arises, all the grasses grow,
and precisely because it obtains autumn, all the myriad treasures are completed.
Surely spring and autumn do not obtain these things without a reason?
The Way of Heaven has already acted.
I have heard that a perfected person dwells like a corpse in a small, enclosed room,
while the common people go wild,
not knowing where to go.
Now, these petty people of Wèilěi 畏壘
are secretly trying to rank me among the worthies to be sacrificed to.
Am I someone fit to be ladled into the pot [like sacrificial meat]?
This is why I am not pleased with the words of Lǎo Dān 老聃."
His disciple said:
"That is not right.
In a ditch of ordinary depth,
large fish have no way to turn their bodies,
and minnows dominate it;
on hills of eight feet in height,
large beasts have no place to hide their bodies,
And the yàohú (㜸狐) takes this as an auspicious omen.
Moreover, to honor the worthy and entrust the able,
to prioritize goodness and benefit,
has been the way since the ancient Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜).
How much more so should the people of Wèilěi (畏壘) follow this principle!
Master, please listen to this!"
Gēngsāngzi (庚桑子) said:
"Young man, come here!
A beast large enough to fill a carriage,
if separated from the mountains,
cannot escape the misfortune of nets and snares;
a fish large enough to swallow a boat,
if stranded and loses water,
can be tormented by ants.
Therefore, birds and beasts are never satisfied with heights,
fish and turtles are never satisfied with depths.
Those who preserve their embodied life,
hide themselves,
and are never satisfied with merely being deeply hidden.
Furthermore, what is so worthy of praise in these two gentlemen?
What is there to commend in these two men?
In their debates,
they will foolishly bore through walls
and plant weeds.
Separating hairs to comb them,
counting grains of rice to cook them,
how can such petty actions possibly benefit the world?
Promoting the worthy
then the people will oppress each other;
if people are trusted to be wise,
then the people will steal from each other.
Such numerical things
are not sufficient to enrich the people.
The people are extremely diligent when it comes to profit;
sons will kill their fathers,
ministers will kill their rulers,
in broad daylight they will be thieves,
in the middle of the day they will dig through walls.
I tell you,
the root of great chaos
will surely arise in the time of Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜,
and its end will exist a thousand generations later.
A thousand generations later,
there will surely be people who eat each other!"
Nánróng Chú 南榮趎 shuddered and sat up straight, saying:
"Given my age,
where shall I entrust my work to understand these words?"
Gēng Sāngzǐ 庚桑子 said:
"Preserve your form,
embrace your life,
do not let your thoughts be restless.
If you do this for three years,
then you can understand these words."
Nánróng Chú 南榮趎 said:
"Eyes and form,
I don't know their difference,
And the blind cannot see themselves;
as for the ear and the form,
I do not know their difference,
and the deaf cannot hear themselves;
as for the mind and the form,
I do not know their difference,
and the mad cannot attain themselves.
The difference between forms is also clear,
but might things interfere with them,
so that they desire to seek each other
but cannot obtain each other?
Now I say to Nánróng Chú:
“Preserve your form,
embrace your life,
do not let your thoughts scheme busily.”
Nánróng Chú, strive to hear the Dao with your ears!"
Gēngsāng Zǐ said: "My words are exhausted.
It is said
that a foraging bee cannot transform into a caterpillar,
a Yuè chicken cannot hatch a swan's egg,
but a Lǔ chicken certainly can.
Chickens and chickens, their virtue is not different,
but there are those who can and those who cannot,
their talent is inherently great or small.
Now my talent is small,
insufficient to transform you.
Why don't you go south to see Lǎozǐ!"
Nánróng Chú prepared provisions,
He traveled for seven days and seven nights to the place of Lǎo Zǐ.
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"Did you come from the land of Chǔ?"
Nánróng Chú said: "Yes."
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"Why are you accompanied by such a crowd of people?"
Nánróng Chú fearfully looked behind him.
Lǎo Zǐ said: "Do you not understand what I mean?"
Nánróng Chú lowered his head in shame,
and looking up, sighed and said:
"Now I have forgotten my answer,
and consequently lost my question."
Lǎo Zǐ said: "What do you mean?"
Nánróng Chú said:
"If I do not know, people call me stupid.
If I know,
it troubles my body instead.
If I am not benevolent, I harm others;
if I am benevolent, it troubles my own body instead.
If I am not righteous, I injure others;
if I am righteous, it troubles myself instead.
Where can I escape to be alright?
These three sayings are what trouble Chú.
I wish to ask about them because of my origins in Chǔ."
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"Earlier I saw between your eyebrows
and therefore I understood you.
Now you speak and believe it.
If you are meticulously proper as if mourning your parents,
it is like raising a pole to seek something in the sea.
You are a lost person,
bewildered!
You want to revert to your true nature
but have no way to enter,
pitiful indeed!"
Nán Róng Chú requested to enter and reside in his house,
summoning what he liked,
removing what he disliked,
for ten days to relieve his sorrow,
and then he saw Lǎozi again.
Lǎozi said:
"You have washed yourself,
yet how melancholy!
And yet within you is still a lively concern,
there is still dislike.
Those who are obstructed externally cannot be grasped with complexity,
for this will block internally;
those who are obstructed internally cannot be grasped with confusion,
for this will block externally.
Those who are obstructed both externally and internally,
morality and virtue cannot hold them,
how much less those who abandon the Dao and act!"
Nán Róng Chú said:
"If a villager is sick,
and the villagers ask about it,
the sick person can describe their illness,
However, being troubled by one's troubles is still not yet being truly troubled.
If what Chú heard was the Great Dao,
it would be like taking medicine to worsen an illness.
Chú would rather hear about the principles of preserving life."
Lǎozǐ said:
"The principles of preserving life—
can you embrace the One?
Can you avoid losing it?
Can you know good and bad fortune without divination?
Can you stop?
Can you cease?
Can you abandon seeking from others and seek from yourself?
Can you be free and unfettered?
Can you be simple and genuine?
Can you be like a child?
A child howls all day long
and his throat does not become hoarse;
this is the perfection of harmony.
He grasps all day long
and his hand does not clench;
this is sharing in virtue.
He stares all day long and his eyes do not blink;
his focus is not on the outside.
He walks without knowing where he is going,
he dwells without knowing what he is doing,
he meanders with things,
and flows with their waves.
These are the principles of preserving life."
Nánróng Chú said,
"Then is this the virtue of the ultimate person?"
He said,
"No.
This is what is called the melting of ice and the thawing of the frozen;
is it capable of [achieving perfection]? For the ultimate person
shares food from the earth with each other
and shares joy in the heavens,
and does not let the benefits and harms of things and people entangle him.
They do not regard each other as strange,
do not scheme with each other,
do not work with each other.
They drift away in a carefree manner,
and arrive in a simple and honest way.
This is called the classic of nurturing life."
He said,
"Then is this the ultimate state?"
He said,
"Not yet.
I have already told you,
'Can you become like a child?'
A child acts without knowing what he is doing,
walks without knowing where he is going,
his body is like a branch of dried wood,
and his heart is like dead ashes.
If one is like this,
misfortune will not come,
nor will fortune arrive.
"Good fortune and misfortune do not exist;
calamity comes from evil people!"
What Yǔ Tàidìng 宇泰定 establishes
originates from the light of Heaven.
What originates from the light of Heaven
allows people to see humanity (in others).
If someone cultivates themselves,
then they will possess constancy.
Those who possess constancy
may be abandoned by people,
but Heaven will assist them.
Those whom people abandon
are called "people of Heaven;"
those whom Heaven assists
are called "Son of Heaven."
Learning involves
learning what cannot be learned;
acting involves
acting on what cannot be acted on;
arguing involves
arguing about what cannot be argued about.
To know to stop at what cannot be known
is the ultimate;
if there is something that is not immediately so,
the balance of Heaven will destroy it.
Preparing objects to shape a form,
concealing against the unforeseen to give rise to thought,
revering the center to reach the other shore—
If so, when all evils arrive,
it is all from Heaven,
and not from man.
It is not enough to cause smoothness;
it cannot enter within the líng tái (靈臺, spiritual platform).
The líng tái (靈臺) has something it holds,
but it does not know what it holds,
and it is something that cannot be held.
Not seeing its sincerity and then acting,
every action is inappropriate.
Deeds enter and do not leave,
each time turning into further loss.
Those who do evil in the clear light,
people can punish them;
those who do evil in the hidden darkness,
spirits can punish them.
Understanding people, understanding spirits,
only then can one walk alone.
Those who are bound within,
act in obscurity;
those who are bound without,
are focused on future expenses.
Those who act in obscurity,
only in mediocrity is there light;
those who focus on future expenses,
are only merchants.
People see their tiptoeing,
It is just like the headman.
Those who are at their wits' end with things,
things enter into them.
Those who are at odds with things,
if their own bodies cannot accommodate,
how can they accommodate others!
Those who cannot accommodate others have no kin.
Those who have no kin are exhausted by others.
No weapon is more destructive than the will;
even the Móyé (鏌鎁) swords are inferior.
No robber is greater than the Yīn-Yáng;
there is nowhere to escape between Heaven and Earth.
It is not that the Yīn-Yáng harm them,
but the mind causes it.
When the Dào (道) is unified,
its division also occurs.
Its completion also occurs, and its completion is also destruction.
The reason for what is to be divided is
its division is for preparation.
The reason for what is to be prepared is
its existence is for preparation.
Therefore, going out and not returning,
one sees one's ghost.
Going out and obtaining,
this is called obtaining death.
Extinguishing and having substance,
is one of the ghosts.
The formless is determined by using the tangible to represent it.
It exits without origin,
and enters without an opening.
That which exits without an opening
possesses substance; possessing substance yet having no location,
and having length yet no origin or tip. Having substance yet having no location
is *yǔ* (宇, space).
Having length yet no origin or tip
is *zhòu* (宙, time).
There is birth,
there is death,
there is exit,
there is entry,
and in entry and exit, one does not see its form.
This is called the Gate of Heaven.
The Gate of Heaven is non-existence;
all things emerge from non-existence.
Existence cannot take existence as existence;
it must emerge from non-existence,
and non-existence returns to non-existence.
The sage conceals himself within this.
The knowledge of the ancients
reached a certain point.
To what point did it reach?
Some believed that there was a time before the existence of things;
this is the ultimate point,
It is exhaustive,
nothing can be added to it.
The next level believes there are things,
treating life as loss,
and death as return.
This is why they are divided.
The next level says
initially there was nothing,
then life came into being,
life quickly leads to death;
taking nothingness as the head,
life as the body,
and death as the tail.
Who knows the one principle governing existence, non-existence, death, and life?
I would befriend him.
These three, though different,
are all of the same clan,
like Zhāo and Jǐng,
Zhù and Dài,
Jiǎ and Shì,
Zhù and Fēng;
they are not one and the same.
There is life, then it is covered in soot (dust),
scattered
called something shifted.
Once they say something shifted,
it is not what they are saying.
Although it is unknowable.
The la sacrifices have animal organs (pí hāi);
they can be scattered and yet cannot be scattered.
The one who inspects the house
tours the ancestral temples,
and also goes to the place where the coffin lies,
in order to move it.
Please, let me try to explain the principle of "moving the 'this'".
Therefore, they take life as fundamental,
and knowledge as the teacher;
relying on this to judge right and wrong.
If there is a name, there must be a corresponding reality;
they use themselves as collateral;
causing others to consider their principles as constant,
and repaying their principles with death.
If this is the case,
they take usefulness as knowledge,
and uselessness as foolishness,
penetration as reputation,
and poverty as disgrace.
"Moving the 'this'"
is the way of the present-day person.
It is like the cicada and the turtledove
agreeing in their similarity.
If you step on someone's foot in the marketplace,
you apologize with a casual excuse;
to an elder brother, you offer solicitous care;
The Great Parent is all.
Therefore it is said:
Utmost propriety contains that which is not humane,
utmost righteousness contains that which is not material,
utmost knowledge contains that which is not scheming,
utmost benevolence contains that which is without intimacy,
utmost trustworthiness shuns gold.
To exhaust the will's rising (勃, bó),
to resolve the mind's errors (謬, miù),
to remove the burden of virtue,
to clear the obstruction of the Dao.
Nobility, wealth, prominence, authority, fame, profit—these six
are the will's risings.
Appearance, movement, color, principle, energy, intention—these six
are the mind's errors.
Hatred, desire, joy, anger, grief, pleasure—these six
are the burden of virtue.
Leaving, approaching,
taking, giving, knowing, ability—these six
are the obstruction of the Dao.
If these four sets of six do not surge through the breast,
then one is correct,
if one is correct, then one is still,
if one is still, then one is clear,
if one is clear, then one is empty,
if one is empty, then one achieves non-action
and yet there is nothing that is not achieved.
The Dao is the ultimate respect for virtue;
Life is the radiance of virtue;
nature is the substance of life.
The movement of nature is called action;
the artificiality of action is called loss.
Knowing is connecting;
knowing is planning.
What the knowing person does not know
is like a sidelong glance.
Acting out of necessity is called virtue;
acting with nothing outside oneself is called governance.
Names are contrary, but reality is harmonious.
Yì (羿) was skilled at hitting subtle targets
but clumsy at making people praise him without reserve.
The sage is skilled in Heaven
but clumsy in human affairs.
Now, to be skilled in Heaven
and good to people,
only a complete person can do this.
Only a worm can be a worm;
only a worm can act as Heaven.
Why would a complete person hate Heaven?
Hate the Heaven of people?
And moreover, would I rather have Heaven or people?
If a single sparrow suited Yì (羿),
Yì (羿) would surely get it;
this is power.
If the whole world were used as a cage,
Then the sparrow has nowhere to escape.
Therefore, Tāng used a cook to trap Yī Yǐn,
and Duke Mù of Qín used the skin of five sheep to trap Bǎilǐ Xī.
Therefore, if you don't use what they like to trap them,
there is no way to obtain them.
Armored warriors shift their plans,
and do not seek external praise;
condemned laborers climb heights without fear,
forgetting life and death.
The brooding hen does not feed and forgets people,
forgetting people,
and therefore becomes a divine being.
Therefore, to respect him
without joy,
to insult him
without anger,
only those who are in harmony with the harmony of Heaven are like this.
To express anger from non-anger,
then anger comes from non-anger;
to express action from non-action,
then action comes from non-action.
To desire stillness, then harmonize your breath;
to desire spirit, then follow your heart;
this is acting with a purpose.
To desire correctness, then rely on what cannot be avoided,
the category of the unavoidable,
is the way of the sage.
Chapter 24: Xú Wúguǐ
Xú Wúguǐ, through Nǚ Shāng, sought an audience with Marquis Wèi Wǔ.
Marquis Wèi Wǔ greeted him, saying:
"Sir, you are weary!
Tired from the toil of the mountains and forests,
hence you are willing to see me."
Xú Wúguǐ said: "I am weary on your account,
but how are you weary on my account!
If you indulge your desires
and prolong your likes and dislikes,
then the true nature of your life will be ill;
if you reject your desires
and suppress your likes and dislikes,
then your ears and eyes will be ill.
I am toiling for you;
how are you toiling for me!"
Marquis Wǔ remained silent, looking detached.
After a short while,
Xú Wúguǐ said:
"Let me tell you about my judging of dogs.
The lowest quality
is content to stop when full;
this is the virtue of a wildcat.
The middling quality is like looking at the sun.
The highest quality seems to be missing something.
My judging of dogs is not as good as my judging of horses.
When I judge horses,
the straight ones are in line with the plumb line,
the curved ones are in line with the hook,
the square ones are in line with the square,
the round ones are in line with the compass.
These are national horses,
but they are not as good as the horses of the world.
The horses of the world
possess potential,
as if cherishing, as if losing,
as if losing a part of themselves.
Horses such as these
surpass and outstrip the dust,
and one does not know where they are."
Wǔ Hóu was greatly pleased and laughed.
Xú Wúguǐ left,
and Nǚ Shāng said:
"Sir, how did you manage to please our lord?
The ways I please our lord
is by speaking horizontally with the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, and *Yuè*
and speaking vertically with the *Jīnbǎn* and *Liù Tāo*.
The services I have rendered with great merit are countless,
and yet our lord has never opened his mouth in praise.
How did you please our lord today, making him so delighted?"
Xú Wúguǐ said:
"I simply told him about my judging of dogs and horses."
Nǚ Shāng said, "Is that so?"
He said, "Have you not heard of the exiled people of Yuè?
After leaving their country for a few days,
they rejoice upon seeing someone they know;
after leaving their country for ten days or a month,
they rejoice upon seeing something they used to see in their country;
and by the time a year has passed,
they rejoice upon seeing someone who resembles a person.
Does not the longer one is away from people,
the deeper one's longing for them becomes?
Those who flee into emptiness,
with weeds and brambles supporting them along the paths of weasels and rats,
stumble about in that emptiness,
and rejoice at the sound of approaching footsteps.
How much more so would they rejoice at the sound of their siblings and relatives clearing their throats nearby!
It has been a long time since the words of a true person have been heard clearing their throat near my lord!"
Xú Wúguǐ met with Marquis Wǔ.
Marquis Wǔ said, "Sir, living in the mountains and forests,
eating acorns and chestnuts,
tiring of onions and chives,
to be a guest of this humble person,
it has been a long time!
Are you now old?
Do you now desire the taste of wine and meat?
Or does this humble person also have the blessings of the state?"
Xú Wúguǐ said,
"Wúguǐ was born in poverty and lowliness,
and has never dared to eat and drink your wine and meat,
"In the future, I will trouble you, sir."
The ruler said, "What is it?
How will I trouble this insignificant person?"
He said, "I will trouble your spirit and form."
Wǔ Hóu said, "What do you mean?"
Xú Wúguǐ said:
"The nourishment of Heaven and Earth is uniform.
Ascending to a high place does not make one taller,
and residing in a low place does not make one shorter.
You alone are the lord of ten thousand chariots,
using the hardship of the people of a whole country
to nourish your ears, eyes, nose, and mouth.
Now, the spirit does not allow itself to be like this.
The spirit
loves harmony and hates wickedness.
Wickedness is a disease,
therefore it troubles the spirit.
Only you, the ruler, are troubled by it; what is the reason?"
Wǔ Hóu said:
"I have long desired to see you, sir.
I wish to love the people and, for the sake of righteousness, cease warfare.
Is this permissible?"
Xú Wúguǐ said, "It is not permissible.
Loving the people
is the beginning of harming the people.
Ceasing warfare for the sake of righteousness
is the root of creating weapons.
If you do these things yourself,
Otherwise, it would probably not be accomplished.
All accomplishments of beauty
are evil instruments.
Even if you, my lord, act with benevolence and righteousness,
it will almost certainly be false!
Form inevitably creates form,
accomplishment inevitably invites boasting,
change inevitably invites external battles.
Your Lordship must not arrange ranks of soaring cranes between the beautiful towers,
nor hoard fine steeds in the palaces of Zītán (錙壇),
nor harbor rebellion in gain,
nor use skill to overcome others,
nor use schemes to overcome others,
nor use war to overcome others.
If killing the people and soldiers,
seizing the land of others,
to nourish my own desires and my own spirit,
in such a war, who knows which side is good?
Where does victory lie?
If you, my lord, cannot stop,
cultivate sincerity in your heart,
to respond to the feelings of heaven and earth, and do not offend them.
When the people die, they are already free.
How will you then use the laying down of arms!"
The Huángdì (黃帝) was about to meet Dàwěi (大隗) on Mount Jùcí (具茨).
Fāngmíng (方明) was the driver,
Chāngyǔ (昌㝢) was the second charioteer,
Zhāng Ruò (張若) and Xì Péng (謵朋) led the horses,
Kūn Hún's jesting rear chariot;
arriving at the wilderness of Xiāngchéng,
the seven sages were all lost,
with nowhere to inquire about the path.
They happened to encounter a shepherd boy,
and asked him for directions.
He said:
"Do you know Mount Jùcí?"
They said:
"Yes."
"Do you know where Dàwěi resides?"
They said:
"Yes."
Huángdì said:
"Extraordinary, little boy!
Not only do you know Mount Jùcí,
but you also know where Dàwěi resides.
I would like to ask you about governing the world."
The little boy said:
"Governing the world,
is just like this,
what else is needed!
Since I was young, I have traveled freely within the six directions.
I once had a disease that caused blurred vision,
and an elder taught me, saying:
'You should ride the chariot of the sun
and travel in the wilderness of Xiāngchéng.'
Now my illness is somewhat better,
I shall once again travel beyond the six directions.
Governing the world is just like this.
Why should I bother with it!"
Huángdì said:
"Indeed, governing the world
is truly not something for you to do.
However,
may I ask about governing the world?"
The young boy declined.
Huángdì asked again.
The young boy said:
"Governing the world,
what difference is there from herding horses?
Simply remove those that harm the horses, that's all!"
Huángdì bowed twice and kowtowed, addressing him as "Heavenly Teacher" and withdrew.
A wise man is unhappy without changes in his thoughts and considerations;
an eloquent man is unhappy without the order of discussion and persuasion;
a discerning man is unhappy without matters of criticism and censure;
all are constrained by things.
Those who attract the world promote the court;
those who are of the middle class glorify officialdom;
those who have physical strength pride themselves on difficulties;
those who are brave exert themselves in adversity;
those who deal in military affairs enjoy war;
those who are withered and old seek lasting fame;
those who are versed in law expand governance;
those who are versed in ritual and education respect appearance;
A person of rén and yì values the opportunity to associate with others.
If a farmer has no weeding and cultivation to do, he has nothing to compare himself to;
if a merchant has no market transactions, he has nothing to compare himself to.

a moment ago you were sitting,
and now you are standing;
a moment ago you were walking,
and now you are still;
what is the reason for this?"
Shadow said:
"I am merely an appendage;
why do you ask such trivial questions?
I exist, but I do not know the reason why.
I am like a cicada's shell, like a snake's slough;
similar, yet not the same.
Fire and the sun,
I hoard them;
shade and night,
I alternate with them.
Are those things what I depend on?
How much more so, those who are without dependence!
When they come, then I come with them;
when they go, then I go with them;
when they are strongly Yang, then I am strongly Yang with them.
Those who are strongly Yang, what is there to ask them!"
Yáng Zǐjū went south to Pèi;
Lǎodān traveled west to Qín.
He was met in the suburbs
and reached Liáng, where he encountered Lǎozǐ.
Lǎozǐ, midway, looked up to the sky and sighed, saying,
"At first, I thought you were teachable,
but now you are not."
Yáng Zǐjū did not reply.
Upon arriving at the lodging,
he presented washing water, a towel, and a comb;
he took off his shoes outside the door,
crawled forward on his knees and said,
"Earlier, this disciple wished to ask you, Master,
but you, Master, were constantly on the move,
and so I dared not.
Now you are free,
He asked about his faults.
Lǎozǐ said:
"You are so arrogant and overbearing, staring and glaring;
with whom do you dwell?
The greatest purity seems like disgrace,
the fullest virtue seems like inadequacy."
Yángzǐ Jū was startled and changed his expression, saying:
"I respectfully receive your instruction!"
When he went [there before],
the innkeeper welcomed him forward,
his family's elder held the mat,
his wife held the towel and comb,
the innkeeper avoided the mat,
and the cook avoided the stove.
When he returned [after the instruction],
the innkeeper contended with him for the mat.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: Abdicating the Throne
Yáo offered the empire to Xǔ Yóu,
but Xǔ Yóu refused.
He then offered it to Zǐzhōu Zhīfù,
Zǐzhōu Zhīfù said:
"To make me the Son of Heaven,
that is indeed permissible.
However, I happen to have a sickness of melancholy,
and I am about to treat it;
I have no time to govern the empire."
The empire is the most weighty thing,
and does not harm his life for it,
how much more so with other things!
Only one who does nothing to (for the sake of) the world,
can be entrusted with the world.
Shùn yielded the world to Zǐzhōu Zhībó.
Zǐzhōu Zhībó said:
"I happen to have a hidden worry and sickness,
and I am about to treat it;
I have not the leisure to govern the world."
Therefore, the world is a great vessel,
but it is not to be exchanged for life;
this is how those who possess the Dao differ from common people.
Shùn yielded the world to Shàn Juǎn,
Shàn Juǎn said:
"I stand within the universe,
in winter I wear furs and skins,
in summer I wear coarse and fine hemp;
in spring I plow and sow,
my body is sufficiently employed in labor;
in autumn I harvest and store,
my body is sufficiently at rest and nourished;
at sunrise I work,
at sunset I rest,
carefree between heaven and earth
and my mind is content.
What use do I have for the world!
Alas,
you do not understand me!"
Thereupon, he refused.
Consequently, he departed and entered the deep mountains,
and no one knew where he was.
Shùn offered the empire to his friend, the farmer of Shíhù.
The farmer of Shíhù said:
"How diligent is the sovereign as a person!
He is a man who cherishes power!"
Considering Shùn's virtue to be insufficient,
thereupon the husband carried his wife on his back and the wife carried their child on her head,
taking them into the sea,
never to return for the rest of their lives.
Dà Wáng Dǎnfù resided in Bīn.
The Dí people attacked him.
He served them with hides and silk,
but they did not accept it.
He served them with dogs and horses,
but they did not accept it.
He served them with pearls and jade,
but they did not accept it.
What the Dí people sought was land.
Dà Wáng Dǎnfù said:
"To live with someone's elder brother
and kill his younger brother,
to live with someone's father
To kill his son,
I cannot bear it.
You must all strive to stay!
What difference is there between being my subject and being a Dí 狄人 subject?
Moreover, I have heard it said,
"One should not harm that which one nourishes with that which one uses."
Thereupon, he leaned on his staff and departed.
The people linked arms and followed him,
and consequently, they established a state at the foot of Mount Qí 岐山.
Now, Tài Wáng Dǎnfù 太王亶父,
can be said to be one who was able to value life.
One who is able to value life,
even if wealthy and noble,
does not harm his body with indulgence;
even if poor and lowly,
does not burden his form with profit.
People of the present age
who hold high offices and esteemed ranks
all greatly fear losing them,
and seeing profit, lightly sacrifice their bodies.
Are they not deluded!
The people of Yuè 越, for three generations, assassinated their ruler.
Prince Sōu 搜 was troubled by this
and fled to the Dān Xué 丹穴 cave.
But the state of Yuè 越 was without a ruler.
They sought Prince Sōu 搜 but could not find him,
so they followed him to Dān Xué 丹穴.
Prince Sōu 搜 would not come out,
so the people of Yuè 越 smoked him out with wormwood.
Then they brought a jade carriage.
Prince Sōu 搜 grasped the carriage rope and boarded the chariot,
looking up to the sky and cried out,
"Lord! O Lord!
Couldn't you have just left me alone!"
Wángzǐ Sōu did not dislike becoming a ruler,
He disliked the troubles of being a ruler.
One like Wángzǐ Sōu,
Can be said not to harm his life for the sake of the state.
This is indeed what the Yuè people wanted as their ruler.
Hán and Wèi were mutually contending to invade land.
Zǐ Huázi met with Zhāo Xī Hóu,
And Zhāo Xī Hóu had a worried expression.
Zǐ Huázi said:
"Now, suppose the world wrote an inscription before you,
The inscription saying:
'If the left hand grasps it, then the right hand will be crippled,
If the right hand grasps it, then the left hand will be crippled,
Yet, whoever grasps it will surely possess the world.'
Would you be able to grasp it?"
Zhāo Xī Hóu said: "I would not grasp it."
Zǐ Huázi said: "Excellent!
From this perspective,
Two arms are more important than the world,
And the body is more important than two arms.
Hán is much lighter than the world,
Nowadays, what people contend for
is even lighter than Hàn and further away.
You, my lord, are indeed worrying yourself and harming your life
by grieving over what you cannot obtain!"
Xī Hóu said: "Excellent!
Many have instructed me,
but I have never heard these words."
Zǐ Huázi can be said
to know what is light and what is heavy.
The ruler of Lǔ heard that Yán Hé was a man who had attained the Dao,
and sent someone with gifts to him in advance.
Yán Hé was guarding a humble lane,
wearing hemp clothing and personally feeding his ox.
The messenger of the ruler of Lǔ arrived,
and Yán Hé himself answered him.
The messenger said: "Is this the home of Yán Hé?"
Yán Hé replied: "This is Hé's home."
The messenger presented the gifts,
and Yán Hé replied:
"I fear that the listener will misunderstand
and cause the messenger to be blamed,
it would be better to verify it."
The messenger returned
and verified it again,
and came back to seek him,
but could no longer find him.
Therefore, someone like Yán Hé,
非 è fùguì yě, / yóu zhòngshēng è zhī yě.
Therefore it is said:
"The essence of the Dao
is used to govern oneself,
its surplus
is used to govern the state,
and its dregs are used to govern the world."
From this perspective,
the accomplishments of emperors and kings
are merely the surplus affairs of sages,
not the means to perfect oneself and nourish life.
The gentlemen of the present age
often endanger and abandon their lives
to sacrifice themselves for material things,
is this not lamentable!
All actions of sages
necessarily examine what they are going to
and what they are doing it for.
Now, suppose there is someone here
who uses the pearl of Marquis Suí to shoot at a sparrow a thousand fathoms high,
the world would certainly laugh at him.
Why is that?
It is because what he uses is valuable
and what he seeks is trivial.
Now, life,
how can it be merely as valuable as the pearl of Marquis Suí!
Master Lièzi was impoverished,
His countenance bore the marks of hunger.
A guest spoke of this
to Zhèng Zǐyáng, saying:
"Liè Yǔkòu,
he is likely a man of Dao,
residing in your state yet impoverished.
Are you not, perhaps, failing to appreciate scholars?"
Zhèng Zǐyáng immediately ordered an official to send him grain.
Zǐ Lièzi came out to see the messenger,
bowed twice, and declined the gift.
After the messenger left,
Zǐ Lièzi entered [his house],
his wife, seeing him, beat her chest and said:
"I heard that the wives and children of those who possess the Dao
all live in ease and pleasure,
yet now we bear the marks of hunger.
The ruler, taking pity, sent food to you, sir,
but you did not accept it.
Is this not our fate!"
Zǐ Lièzi laughed and said to her:
"The ruler does not know me himself.
He sent me grain based on the words of others.
When it comes to blaming me,
he will also rely on the words of others.
This is why I did not accept it."
In the end, the people indeed caused trouble and killed Zǐyáng.
When King Zhāo of Chǔ lost his kingdom,
Tú Yáng Yuè fled
and followed King Zhāo of Chǔ.
King Zhāo returned to his kingdom,
and was about to reward his followers,
including Tú Yáng Yuè.
Tú Yáng Yuè said:
"When the King lost his kingdom,
I, Yuè, lost my butchering.
Now that the King has returned to his kingdom,
I, Yuè, have also returned to my butchering.
My official position and salary have already been restored,
so what reward is there to be had!"
The King said: "Insist on it!"
Tú Yáng Yuè said:
"When the King lost his kingdom,
it was not my fault,
so I did not dare submit to the punishment;
now that the King has returned to his kingdom,
it is not my merit,
so I dare not accept the reward."
The King said: "Grant him an audience!"
Tú Yáng Yuè said:
"The laws of the State of Chǔ
require that one must have great rewards for great merit
before being granted an audience.
Now, my wisdom is insufficient to preserve the kingdom,
and my courage is insufficient to fight to the death against the enemy.
When the Wú army entered Yǐng,
I, Yuè, feared difficulty
and avoided the enemy,
I did not deliberately follow the King.
Now, the King
wishes to abandon the law and break the agreement to grant me an audience,
this is not what I have heard of him doing in the world."
The King said to Sīmǎ Zǐqí:
"Túyáng Yuè lives in humble circumstances,
but his statements of righteousness are very lofty.
Please, on my behalf, invite him with the position of Three Banners."
Túyáng Yuè said:
"The position of Three Banners,
I know is more esteemed than my butcher's stall;
a salary of ten thousand *zhōng*,
I know is richer than the profit from my butchery;
but how can I covet rank and salary
and cause my lord to have a reputation for reckless bestowal!
Yuè dares not accept it;
I wish to return to my butcher's stall."
And so he did not accept it.
Yuán Xiàn lived in Lǔ,
in a room surrounded by earthen walls,
thatched with growing grass;
the rush door was incomplete,
with mulberry wood as its pivot; / with broken jars as windows in two rooms,
and coarse hemp cloth as a covering;
the roof leaked above and it was damp below, / yet he sat upright and played the lute.
Zǐ Gòng rode a large horse, / the inner garment dark red and the outer white.
The carriage could not fit in the alley.
He went to see Yuán Xiàn.
Yuán Xiàn wore a flowered hat and loose slippers,
leaning on a staff to answer the door.
Zǐ Gòng said, / "Alas!
What illness does the master have?"
Yuán Xiàn replied,
"I have heard that,
having no wealth is called poverty,
learning but not being able to put it into practice is called illness.
Now I am poor, not ill."
Zǐ Gòng hesitated and looked ashamed.
Yuán Xiàn laughed and said,
"To act seeking worldly fame,
to form cliques and make friends,
to learn for the sake of others,
to teach for oneself,
the pretenses of benevolence and righteousness,
the adornments of carriages and horses,
I cannot bear to do them."
Zēngzǐ lived in Wèi,
wearing a hemp robe without an outer lining,
his face swollen and gaunt,
his hands and feet calloused.
For three days, he did not light a fire,
for ten years, he did not make clothes,
when he straightened his hat, the tassel broke,
To adjust one's collar only to reveal the elbow,
to put on shoes only to have the heel burst through.
To drag slippers and sing the "Shang Song,"
the sound fills heaven and earth,
as if emanating from metal and stone.
The Son of Heaven cannot make him his subject;
the feudal lords cannot make him their friend.
Therefore, one who cultivates the will forgets the body;
one who nourishes the body forgets profit;
one who embodies the Dao forgets the mind.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said to Yán Huí 顏回:
"Huí 回, come!
Your family is poor and your dwelling humble,
why not take office?"
Yán Huí 顏回 replied,
"I do not wish to take office.
I have fifty *mǔ* of fields outside the city wall,
enough to provide gruel and rice;
ten *mǔ* of fields inside the city wall,
enough for silk and hemp;
playing the zither is enough to amuse myself;
and what I have learned from the Master's Dao
is enough to delight myself.
I do not wish to take office."
Kǒngzǐ 孔子, with a worried expression, changed his countenance and said,
"Excellent, the intention of Huí 回!
I have heard it said,
"Those who know contentment
do not burden themselves with profit;
those who carefully understand what they have obtained
are not afraid of losing it;
those who cultivate themselves internally
are not ashamed even without high position."
Qiū (丘, Confucius) has recited this for a long time,
but only now, with Huí (回, referring to Yan Hui), do I truly understand it.
This is something I, Qiū, have gained."
Gōngzǐ Mù (公子牟) of Zhōngshān (中山) said to Zhān Zǐ (瞻子):
"My body is on the rivers and seas,
but my heart dwells below the imperial palace of Wèi (魏).
What should I do?"
Zhān Zǐ said: / "Value life.
Valuing life leads to a disregard for profit."
Gōngzǐ Mù of Zhōngshān said:
"Although I know this, / I cannot overcome myself."
Zhān Zǐ said: / "If you cannot overcome yourself, then follow your inclinations."
"How can the spirit be free from harm?"
"If one cannot overcome oneself
but forcibly resists following inclinations,
this is called a severe wound.
A severely wounded person
has no hope of a long life."
Wèi Mù (魏牟),
the son of a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
hiding in caves and mountains is more difficult than for a commoner;
although he has not reached the Dao (道),
It can be said that he had the intention.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 was in dire straits between Chén 陳 and Cài 蔡.
For seven days, he had no cooked food.
His goosefoot soup had no grains added.
His complexion was very weary.
This is the integrity of these two gentlemen.
Dào Zhí, Chapter Twenty-Nine
Kǒngzǐ was friends with Liǔ Xiàjì.
Liǔ Xiàjì's younger brother was named Dào Zhí.
Dào Zhí led nine thousand soldiers,
rampaging across the land,
invading and plundering the various lords,
breaking into houses and prying open doors,
driving away people's cattle and horses,
seizing people's wives and daughters,
greedily acquiring wealth and forgetting his relatives,
not caring for his parents and siblings,
not offering sacrifices to his ancestors.
In every town he passed,
large states defended their cities,
small states retreated to their fortifications,
and the common people suffered greatly.
Kǒngzǐ said to Liǔ Xiàjì:
"A man who is a father
must be able to instruct his son;
a man who is an elder brother
must be able to teach his younger brother.
If a father cannot instruct his son,
and an elder brother cannot teach his younger brother,
then there is no value in the affection between father and son, and brothers.
Now, sir,
you are a talented gentleman of this generation,
My younger brother is Zhí, a robber,
a scourge to the world,
and I am unable to teach him.
I, Qiū, secretly feel ashamed for you, sir.
I request to go and persuade him for you."
Liǔxià Jì said:
"Sir, you say that one who is a father
is certainly able to instruct his son,
and one who is an elder brother
is certainly able to teach his younger brother.
If the son does not listen to his father's instruction,
and the younger brother does not accept his elder brother's teaching,
even with your eloquence, sir,
what will you be able to do?
Moreover, Zhí's character is such that
his mind is like a gushing spring,
his will is like a whirlwind,
his strength is sufficient to resist enemies,
his eloquence is sufficient to gloss over wrongdoings,
if you follow his inclinations, he is pleased,
if you go against his inclinations, he becomes angry,
and he easily insults people with words.
Sir, you must not go."
Kǒngzǐ did not listen.
Yánhuí acted as the driver,
Zǐgòng was on the right,
and they went to see Dào Zhí.
Dào Zhí was then resting his soldiers on the south side of Mount Tài,
He slices human livers and eats them as provisions.
Kǒngzǐ alighted from his carriage and went forward,
seeing an attendant he said:
"A man from Lǔ, Kǒng Qiū,
has heard of the general's lofty righteousness."
He respectfully bowed twice to the attendant.
The attendant went in to report,
Dào Zhí heard this
and was greatly enraged.
His eyes were like bright stars,
his hair bristled, lifting his cap,
he said:
"Isn't this that crafty and deceitful man from the state of Lǔ, Kǒng Qiū?
Tell him for me:
'You create speeches and fabricate words,
falsely claiming the names of Wén and Wǔ,
wearing a cap of woven branches,
with a belt of dead ox ribs,
using excessive and false speech,
eating without plowing,
wearing clothes without weaving,
wagging your lips and flapping your tongue,
presumptuously creating right and wrong,
in order to delude the lords of the world,
causing the scholars of the world not to return to their roots,
falsely acting filial and fraternal
and hoping to gain favor for marquisates, honors, riches, and nobility.
"Your crimes are extremely grave and heavy.
Flee quickly and return!
If not,
I will use your liver to augment the midday meal!"'
Kǒngzǐ again asked for an audience, saying:
"Qiū has received favor from Jì,
and wishes to wait beneath the curtain."
The attendant again announced him.
Dào Zhí said:
"Have him come forward!"
Kǒngzǐ hastened forward,
avoiding the mat and stepping back,
and bowed twice to Dào Zhí.
Dào Zhí was greatly angered,
stretching out both his legs,
resting his hand on his sword, glaring,
his voice like a tiger cub,
and said:
"Qiū, come forward!
If what you say
accords with my will, then you shall live;
if it goes against my heart, then you shall die."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Qiū has heard that
in all the world there are three virtues:
to be born and grow tall,
beautiful and without equal,
young and old, noble and base,
To be seen and be pleasing to all is
the highest virtue;
to understand the warp and weft of Heaven and Earth,
and to be able to distinguish all things,
is middle virtue;
to be brave and resolute,
to gather a crowd and lead troops,
is the lowest virtue.
Any person possessing one of these virtues
is sufficient to face south and call himself an orphan (a royal "we").
Now, General, you possess all three of these.
You are eight feet two inches tall,
your face and eyes are radiant,
your lips are like bright cinnabar,
your teeth are like aligned shells,
your voice resonates like the Yellow Bell,
and yet you are called Dào Zhí,
I, Qiū, secretly feel ashamed for the General that you do not take [such a position].
If the General is willing to listen to me,
I request to be sent south to Wú and Yuè,
north to Qí and Lǔ,
east to Sòng and Wèi,
and west to Jìn and Chǔ,
to have them build a great city of several hundred *lǐ* for the General,
and establish a city of several hundred thousand households,
to honor the General as a feudal lord,
to start afresh with the world,
dismiss the troops and let the soldiers rest,
To adopt one's brothers and younger siblings,
and together sacrifice to one's ancestors
—this is the conduct of sages and talented scholars,
and the desire of the world."
Dào Zhí flew into a great rage and said,
"Qiū, come forward!
Those who can be influenced by profit
and persuaded by words
are all what are called foolish and lowly commoners.
Now, to be tall, big, and handsome,
and to be pleasing to people's eyes
—this is the virtue left to me by my parents.
Even if you, Qiū, do not praise me,
how could I not know this myself?
Moreover, I have heard it said that
those who praise people to their faces
also like to slander them behind their backs.
Now you, Qiū, tell me about great cities and crowds of people;
this is wanting to influence me with profit
and keep me as a commoner.
How can that be long-lasting!
Among great cities, / none is greater than the world.
Yáo and Shùn possessed the world,
yet their descendants did not have a place to put a gimlet;
Tāng and Wǔ established themselves as emperors,
but their later generations were extinguished.
Was it not because their profit was too great?
"Moreover, I have heard it said that
In ancient times, there were many animals and birds but few people.
Therefore, the people all lived in nests to avoid them.
During the day, they gathered acorns and chestnuts;
in the evening, they rested on trees.
Therefore, they were called the people of Yǒu Cháo Shì.
In ancient times, the people did not know about clothing.
In summer, they accumulated much firewood;
in winter, they burned it for warmth.
Therefore, they were called
the people who knew how to preserve life.
In the era of Shén Nóng,
when they lay down, they were relaxed and at ease;
when they got up, they were carefree and content.
The people knew their mothers,
but did not know their fathers.
Living with elk and deer,
plowing and eating,
weaving and wearing clothes,
without any intention to harm each other—
this is the height of perfect virtue.
However, Huángdì (黃帝) was unable to achieve such virtue;
he battled Chī Yóu (蚩尤) in the wilderness of Zhuōlù (涿鹿),
and blood flowed for a hundred *lǐ*.
Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) arose,
establishing retinues of officials;
Tāng (湯) banished his lord,
and King Wǔ (武王) killed Zhòu (紂).
From then on,
the strong oppressed the weak,
and the many tyrannized the few.
Ever since Tāng (湯) and King Wǔ (武王),
all have been followers of disorder.
Now, you cultivate the Way of Wén (文) and Wǔ (武),
Yet, he played music and sang in his room.
Yán Huí 顏回 picked vegetables outside.
Zǐlù 子路 and Zǐgòng 子貢 spoke to each other, saying:
"The Master has been twice expelled from Lǔ 魯,
had his tracks erased in Wèi 衛,
had trees felled in Sòng 宋,
was in distress in Shāngzhōu 商周,
was besieged in Chén 陳 and Cài 蔡.
It would be no crime to kill the Master.
There would be no prohibition against insulting the Master.
Playing music and strumming the zither,
his sounds have never ceased.
Is the shamelessness of a gentleman like this?"
Yán Huí 顏回 had no way to respond.
He went inside and told Kǒngzǐ 孔子.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 pushed aside his zither and sighed, saying:
"Yóu 由 and Cì 賜 are small men.
Call them in, I will tell them."
Zǐlù 子路 and Zǐgòng 子貢 entered.
Zǐlù 子路 said:
"In this state, it can be said we are in dire straits!"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"What are you saying!
A *jūnzǐ* (君子) who is versed in the *dào* (道) is said to be successful;
one who is confined by the *dào* is said to be impoverished.
Now, I, Qiū (丘, referring to Kǒngzǐ 孔子), embrace the *dào* of benevolence and righteousness
and encounter the troubles of a chaotic age,
how can that be considered impoverishment!
Therefore, upon introspection, I am not ashamed of the *dào*;
facing hardship, I do not lose my virtue.
When the great cold arrives,
and frost and snow descend,
it is then that I know the flourishing of pines and cypresses.
In the past, Duke Huán (桓公) obtained it in Jǔ (莒),
Duke Wén (文公) obtained it in Cáo (曹),
the King of Yuè (越王) obtained it at Kuàijī (會稽),
and the straits of Chén (陳) and Cài (蔡) -- / for me, Qiū, it is a piece of good fortune!"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) adjusted his zither and began to sing,
while Zǐlù (子路) vigorously grabbed his shield and danced.
Zǐgòng (子貢) said:
"I do not know the height of the heavens,
nor the depth of the earth."
Those in ancient times who attained the *dào*,
were joyful in poverty
and joyful in success.
What they rejoiced in was not poverty or success,
but the *dào* obtained in this,
so poverty and success are one,
like the order of cold, heat, wind, and rain.
Therefore, Xǔ Yóu (許由) found joy in Yǐngyáng (潁陽),
and Gòng Bó (共伯) obtained it at Gòngshǒu (共首).
Shùn (舜) used the empire to defer to his friend Běirén Wúzé (北人无擇),
Běirén Wúzé (北人无擇) said:
"How extraordinary is the successor's character,
便能返回到我就是道，道就是我，我与道合而为一的境界了。
and go against his wishes, and fail to satisfy the Crown Prince below,
then I will be punished and die.
Where would Zhōu 周 find a place to use the gold?
If I, your servant, address the Great King and satisfy the Crown Prince below,
what could the Zhào 赵 state seek that it would not obtain!"
The Crown Prince said, "Indeed.
What my king admires
are swordsmen only."

To speak without discriminating right from wrong is called *yú*.
To be fond of speaking of others' wickedness is called *chán*.
To sow discord and alienate family is called *zéi*.
To praise with deceit and falsehood in order to ruin wicked people is called *tè*.
Without discriminating good from bad,
accommodating both expressions,
stealing and extracting what one desires,
this is called *xiǎn*.
These eight flaws
outwardly disorder others,
inwardly harm oneself;
the *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) does not befriend them,
the enlightened ruler does not employ them.
The so-called four maladies:
To be fond of managing great affairs,
changing and altering what is normal,
in order to gain fame and merit,
this is called *tāo*.
To monopolize knowledge and be arbitrary in action,
to encroach upon others and act only according to oneself,
is called greed (tān);
to not correct mistakes when they are seen,
and to become even worse when advised,
is called obstinacy (hěn);
to deem acceptable only those who agree with oneself,
and those who disagree with oneself,
even if they are good, to deem them bad,
is called arrogance (jīn).
These are the four faults.
If one can eliminate the eight flaws
and refrain from the four faults,
then one can begin to be taught."
Kǒngzǐ looked solemn and sighed,
bowed twice, and rose, saying:
"Qiū was twice driven out of Lǔ,
had his footprints erased in Wèi,
had trees felled in Sòng,
and was surrounded in Chén and Cài.
Qiū does not know what he has lost
that leads to these four slanders being directed at me?"
The guest sadly changed his expression and said:
"How difficult it is for you to awaken!
There is a man who fears his shadow and hates his footprints
and so runs away from them.
The more he lifts his feet,
the more footprints there are.
The faster he ran, the more his shadow stayed with him (his body).
He thought he was still too slow.
He ran faster without stopping.
He exhausted his strength and died.
He did not know to seek shade to rest his shadow,
to seek stillness to cease his tracks.
How foolish indeed!
You examine the space between rén and yì (benevolence and righteousness),
observe the boundaries of sameness and difference,
view the changes of movement and stillness,
moderate the measure of receiving and giving,
manage the feelings of like and dislike,
harmonize the moderation of joy and anger,
and yet you are almost unable to avoid trouble.
Carefully cultivate your body,
cautiously guard its truth (authenticity),
return things to others,
and then you will be free from burdens.
Now you do not cultivate your body
but seek it from others,
is this not external?"
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) turned pale and said:
"May I ask what is meant by 'truth' (authenticity)?"
The guest said:
"Truth,
is the utmost of essence and sincerity.
Without essence and sincerity, one cannot move others.
Therefore, one who forces tears
Though sad, not grieving;
the forcibly angry,
though stern, are not awe-inspiring;
the forcibly affectionate,
though smiling, are not harmonious.
True sorrow is soundless and grieving;
true anger, though not yet expressed, is awe-inspiring;
true affection, though not yet smiling, is harmonious.
When genuineness is within,
the spirit moves outward;
this is why genuineness is valued.
Applied to human affairs,
in serving parents, it is kindness and filial piety;
in serving the ruler, it is loyalty and integrity;
in drinking wine, it is joy and pleasure;
in mourning, it is grief and sorrow.
Loyalty and integrity emphasize accomplishment;
drinking wine emphasizes joy;
mourning emphasizes sorrow;
serving parents emphasizes comfort.
The beauty of accomplished merit
leaves no trace.
Serving parents for comfort
does not dwell on the means;
drinking wine for pleasure
does not select the utensils;
mourning for sorrow
does not question the rites.
Ritual
is what is done by the world;
truth
is what is received from Heaven,
and is naturally unchangeable.
Therefore, the sage models Heaven and values truth,
not being bound by custom.
The foolish are the opposite of this.
They cannot model Heaven
but are concerned with people,
not knowing to value truth,
and they busily receive changes from custom,
therefore they are insufficient.
Alas,
that you, Master, were so early immersed in human artifice
and so late in hearing the Great Dao!"
Kǒngzǐ again bowed twice
and rose, saying:
"Today, Qiū has the good fortune to meet you,
as if Heaven is favoring me.
That you, Master, do not feel ashamed
to compare me to a servant,
and personally teach me.
May I ask where you dwell,
so that I may receive instruction
and complete my study of the Great Dao."
The guest said:
"I have heard that
Those with whom one can go, go with them.
As for the subtle Way,
those with whom one cannot go,
who do not understand its Way,
be very careful not to go with them,
and you will be free from blame.
Strive for it!
I am leaving you,
I am leaving you!"
Then he punted the boat and left,
drifting along among the reeds.
Yán Yuān turned the carriage around,
Zǐlù handed him the rein,
Kǒngzǐ did not look back,
waiting until the ripples on the water had settled
and he could no longer hear the sound of the oars
before he dared to get in the carriage.
Zǐlù, standing by the carriage,
asked, saying:
"Yóu has been serving you for a long time,
and has never seen the Master treat anyone with such deference.
The rulers of ten thousand chariots,
the lords of a thousand chariots,
when they meet the Master,
never fail to divide the court and treat him as an equal,
yet the Master still has an arrogant demeanor.
Now, this fisherman, leaning on his oar and standing against us,
Yet, Master, you bow and bend your body deeply,
speaking and responding with obeisance.
Is this not excessive?
Your disciples all find this strange, Master.
How does this fisherman deserve such treatment?"
Kǒngzǐ, leaning on the carriage rail, sighed and said:
"Yóu, it is indeed difficult to change you!
You have been steeped in ritual and righteousness for some time,
but your crude and boorish heart has yet to be shed.
Come,
let me tell you!
To not respect elders is
a breach of etiquette.
To not honor the worthy is
unkind.
One who is not a truly accomplished person
cannot humble himself before others.
If one's humility is not genuine,
he cannot grasp its true essence,
and therefore will often injure himself.
Alas!
For a person, there is no greater calamity than unkindness,
and Yóu alone embraces it.
Moreover, the Dao
is that by which all things proceed.
Creatures that lose it die,
and those that obtain it live.
Acting against it in any endeavor leads to failure,
Following it leads to success.
Therefore, where the Dao resides,
the sage reveres it.
Now, this fisherman’s understanding of the Dao
can be said to be present.
How dare I not respect him!”
Chapter Thirty-Two: Liè Yǔkòu
Liè Yǔkòu was going to Qí,
but turned back halfway.
He encountered Bó Hūn Màorén.
Bó Hūn Màorén said: "Why are you turning back?"
He said:
"I was startled."
He said:
"What startled you?"
He said:
"I once ate at ten soup stalls,
and five soup stalls served me first."
Bó Hūn Màorén said: "If that is so, then why are you startled?"
He said:
"If inner sincerity is not understood,
and one’s appearance betrays one’s brilliance,
using external things to calm people's hearts,
causing people to slight the honored elders,
and obscuring what troubles them.
The soup-sellers are merely selling soup for a living,
hoping for a little extra profit.
The profit they seek is meager,
and the power they hold is insignificant,
and yet it is like this,
how much more so for the ruler of ten thousand chariots!
One exhausts oneself for the country
and one's wisdom on affairs,
